S.R.O. 4.—In exercise of the powers conferred by the provision to article 309 of the Constitution and in

Operator and Binder) Recruitment Rules, 2007, in so far as these relate to the posts of Hindi Typist, except as respects 
things done or omitted to be done before such supersession, the President hereby make the following rules regulating 
the method of Recruitment for the post of Hindi Typist in the Directorate General of Army Air Defence:- 


l. Short Title and Commencement. - (a) These rules may be called the Ministry of Defence, Directorate 
General of Army Air Defence, Group ‘C’ (Non-Gazetted) (Hindi Typist) Recruitment Rules, 2025.

3. Method of Recruitment, age-limit and other qualifications etc - The method of recruitment, age-limit and 
other matters relating to the said post shall be as specified in Column (5) to (3) of the said Schedule. 


4. Disqualification - No person, - 
(a) Who has entered into or contracted a marriage with a person having a spouse living; or 


(b) Who, having a spouse living, has entered into or contracted a marriage with any person, shall be eligible 
for appointment to the said post: 


Provided that the Central Government may, if satisfied that such marriage is permissible under the personal 
law applicable to such person and the other party to the marriage and that there are other grounds for doing so, exempt 
any person from the operation of this rule. 


5. Power to relax - Where the Central Government is of the opinion that, it is necessary of expedient to do so, 
it may, by order, for reasons to be recorded in writing, relax any of the provisions of these rules with respect to any 
class or category of persons. 

6. Saving - Nothing in these rules shall affect reservations, relaxation of age-limit and other concessions 
required to be provided for the Scheduled Castes, the Schedule Tribes, the Other Backward Classes, the Ex- 
servicemen and other special Categories of persons, in accordance with the orders issued by the Central Government 
from time to time in this regard.

(Passed on this 67 day of October, 2025) 


As per letter dated 07/09/2015 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference 
has been made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’) as per 
Notification No. L-12011/48/2015-(IR(B-I)) dt. 07/09/2015. The dispute under reference relates to:- 


“Whether the action of the management of Narmada Jhabua Gramin Bank in terminating the service of 
workman Shri Shankar Singh Bamaniya w.e.f. 07.10.2014 is justified? If not, what relief the workman 
entitled to?” 


After registering the case on the basis of reference, notices were issued to the parties. They appeared and 
filed their respective statement of claim in defense. 


Facts connected in brief are that the departmental enquiry has been conducted against rules and procedure he 
was not given sufficient opportunity to defend his case. No principle of natural justice is followed in the enquiry. The 
charges were wrongly held proved and punishment is disproportionate to the charges proved. 


According to management, the workman was issued the charge sheet dated 22/03/2013 with an allegation 
that while being posted at the Manawar Branch and Ganpur Branch within the period 15/06/2009 to 17/06/2011 in 
Ganpur Branch and 18/06/2011 to 27/12/2011, he misappropriated Rs 3.84 lakhs from the accounts of various account 
holders. After finding his reply to the charge sheet unsatisfactory the department decided to conduct departmental 
enquiry the enquiry was conducted as per rules and principle of natural justice, given full opportunity to the workman 
to defend his case. The Enquiry Officer submitted his report on 30/07/2024 holding all the charges proved. Agreeing 
with the findings in the enquiry, the disciplinary authority issued show cause notice to the workman with the copy of 
enquiry report and after considering the reply of the workman, punishment of removal of the workman from the 
service of the management bank was passed by the disciplinary authority on 19/09/2014. Also recovery of the amount 
of Rs. 3.84 Lakh, suffered by the bank was directed to be realized from gratuity. Appeal against this order was also 
dismissed by the appellate authority. The charges are proved and punishment is also not disproportionate to the 
charges. २९/05/2015 has been registered on the basis of petition of the workman, filed by him under section 2-A 
(2&3) of the Act against his termination with same allegations. 


These two cases have been consolidated and RC/05/2015 has been merged in the reference case R/85/2015, 
because the parties, dispute and the pleadings were the same. 


Following preliminary issue was framed on the basis of pleadings- 
Whether the enquiry conducted against the workman is legal and proper? 


On the basis of evidence on record, this preliminary issue was decided vide order dated 29.09.2024 holding 
the departmental enquiry legal and proper, this order is part of this judgment and award. 


Following Additional Issues were framed, thereafter:- 

(A) Whether the charges are proved on the basis of enquiry? 

(B) Whether the punishment is proportionate to the charges proved? 
(C) Whether the workmen are entitled for permanent status or not? 
The parties did not file any evidence on these issues. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for workman Mr. Arun Patel and Mr. Aviral Vinayak Jarolia, 
Learned Counsel for the management side. I have gone through the record as well. 


Additional Issue No.1, 


Charges against the workman are total nine, served on him vide show cause notices dated 28.12.2011, 
10.07.2012 and 20.01.2012, charges list dated 28.12.2011 enumerates the following charges. Firstly, while being 
posted as Cashier in the Manawar Branch of the Bank within the period 17.06.2011 to 27.12.2011, he received 
Rs. 25,000/- from the Account Holder, Badrilal to be deposited in the account of account holder on 28.10.2011, he 


7066 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


made entry of this receipt in the passbook of account holder but did not deposit it with the bank and did not make any 
entry in the bank register. Secondly, on 06.09.2011, he received Rs. 23,000/- from Account Holder, Rakesh to be 
deposited in the account of account holder. He made an entry of this deposit in the passbook of the account holder but 
did not deposit it with the bank nor did he make any entry in the bank records in this respect. Thirdly, on 16.09.2011, 
he received Rs. 25,000/- from Account Holder, Shrikrishna to be deposited in his account. He made an entry of this 
deposit in the passbook of the account holder but did not deposit it with the bank and did not make entry in this 
respect. Vide show cause notice dated 10.07.2012 three charges were leveled against him related to the period 
between 15.06.2009 to 17.06.2011 which were firstly, he withdrew Rs. 1 Lac/- from the account of Account Holder, 
Radheshyam on 03.06.2010 by preparing a withdrawal form and forged signature of the account holder on the 
withdrawal form. Secondly, he received Rs. 6,011/- from the Account Holder, Radheshyam to be deposited in his 
account and made entry in this respect in the passbook of the account holder but did not deposit it with the bank and 
also did not make entry of this deposit in the bank register. Thirdly, on 07.05.2011, he received Rs. 1 Lac/- from 
Account Holder, Kailash to be deposited in his account, this time also he made entry of this deposit in the passbook of 
the account holder but did not deposit it with the bank nor did he made any entry of this deposit in the bank records. 
Vide show cause notice dated 20.01.2012, he misappropriated amount of Rs. 45,000/- on 10.10.2011, Rs. 40,000/- on 
05.09.2011 and Rs. 20,000/- on 12.10.2011 from Account Holders, Sitaram, Harishing and Sanjay to be deposited in 
their accounts, he made entry of these deposits in their passbooks but kept the amount with him and did not make 
entry of these deposits in the bank records. 


Learned Counsel for the workman has stated that two criminal trials proceeded on the basis of very same 
charges which resulted into acquittal of the workman and this acquittal was affirmed by Hon’ble Session Court in 
appeal. Judgments on record. 


He further submits that the same set of witnesses were examined during the criminal trial also, hence, the 
report of the enquiry officer, holding the charges proved cannot be held correct in law. Learned Counsel has further 
referred to in the present case only one charge sheet dated 22.03.2013 was issued to the workman for two charges and 
no additional charge sheet was issued to him, whereas the enquiry report dated 30.07.2014 submitted by the enquiry 
officer had finding with respect to seven charges the original two charges were not proved, during the enquiry, hence, 
on this ground also the finding of the enquiry officer is not correct. 


Learned Counsel has referred to judgment of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of State of U.P. vs. Saroj 
Kumar Sinha, (2010) 2 SCC 772, wherein it has been held that the enquiry officer acts as a Quasi-Judicial Authority. 
Learned Counsel for workman has further referred to another judgment of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of 
Roop Singh Negi vs. Punjab National Bank, (2009) 2 SCC 570, in this case also same principle has been laid down. 
In another case, Union of India vs. Vishwanath Chatarjee, Civil Appeal No. 5258/2009, has also been referred to by 
the workman side, in this respect. 


As regards, the first contention of the Learned Counsel for workman that originally two charges were 
levelled and other charges were added later on. I see no illegality in this respect, the department is within its rights to 
add, amend or alter charges on the basis of evidence which surface during course of time. 


There can be no quarrel with the proposition that a departmental enquiry is a quasi-judicial proceeding and 
the enquiry officer is not expected to work as a representative of department rather he has to work independently. 


Further, the settled proposition of law, with respect to proof of charges in a departmental enquiry is different 
from that in a criminal trial. 


Following judgments are being referred to in this respect. 


Scope of disciplinary proceedings and scope of criminal proceedings are quite distinct, exclusive 
and independent of each other. Standards of proof in the two proceedings are also different. Ref. T.N.C.S. 
Corpn. Ltd. vs. K. Meerabai, (2006) 2 SCC 255. 


Standard of proof in a departmental enquiry which is quasicriminal/quasi-judicial in nature: 
Disciplinary proceedings, however, being quasi-criminal in nature, there should be some evidence to prove 
the charge. Although the charges in a departmental proceedings are not required to be proved like a 
criminal trial i.e. beyond all reasonable doubts, we cannot lose sight of the fact that the enquiry officer 
performs a quasijudicial function, who upon analyzing the documents must arrive at a conclusion that there 
had been a preponderance of probability to prove the charges on the basis of materials on record. While 
doing so, he cannot take into consideration any irrelevant fact. He cannot refuse to consider the relevant 
facts. He cannot shift the burden of proof. He cannot reject the relevant testimony of the witnesses only on 
the basis of surmises and conjectures. Ref: (i) Nirmala J. Jhala Vs. State of Gujarat & Another, AIR 2013 
SC 1513 (paras 10, 11, 12 & 13). (ii) M.V. Bijlani Vs. Union of India, (2006) 5 SCC 88 (Para 25) 


In the cases of (i) NOIDA Entrepreneurs Association Vs NOIDA & others, AIR 2007 SC 1161 
(i4i) State Bank of India Vs. R.B. Sharma, (2004) 7 SCC 27 (iii) Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan Vs. T. 
Srinivas, (2004) 7 SCC 442 (iv) Depot Manager, APSRTC Vs. Mohd. Yousuf Miya, (1997) 2 SCC 699 (v) 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7067 


Captain M. Paul Anthony Vs. Bharat Gold Mines Limited (1999) 3 SCC 679 and (vi) State of Rajasthan 
Vs. B.K. Meena, (1996) 6 SCC 417 (vi) Pratap Singh Vs. State of Punjab, AIR 1964 SC 72 (vii) Jang 
Bahadur Singh Vs. Baij Nath, AIR 1969 SC 30, it has been laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court that 
"the purpose of departmental enquiry and of prosecution are two different and distinct aspects. 
Departmental Enquiry is to maintain discipline in the service and efficiency of public service. Crime is an 
act of commission in violation of law or of omission of public duty. The enquiry in a departmental 
proceeding relates to the conduct or breach of duty by the delinquent officer to punish him for his 
misconduct defined under the relevant statutory rules or law. It is the settled legal position that the strict 
standard of proof or applicability of the Evidence Act stands excluded in a departmental proceeding. 
Criminal Proceedings and the departmental proceeding under enquiry can go on simultaneously." 


In the case of T.N.C.S. Corporation Ltd. Vs. K. Meerabai, (2006) 2 SCC 255, it has been held by 
the Hon'ble Supreme Court that the scopes of the disciplinary proceedings and of criminal proceedings are 
quite distinct, exclusive and independent of each other. Standards of proof in the two proceedings are also 


different. 


In the cases of Mohd. Saleem Siddiqui Vs. State of UP & others, (2011) 2 UPLBEC 1575 
(Allahabad High Court) and Ajeet Kumar Naag Vs. General Manager Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. 
Haldia, JT 2005 (8) SC 425, the distinction between departmental enquiry and criminal proceedings has 
been drawn as under: "The two proceedings i.e. criminal and departmental are entirely different. They 
operate in different fields and have different objectives. The object of criminal proceedings is to inflict 
appropriate punishment on offender and the purpose of enquiry proceedings is to deal with the delinquent 
departmentally and to impose penalty in accordance service rules the rule relating to appreciation of 
evidence in the two proceedings is also not similar. In criminal law burden of proof is on the prosecution and 
unless the prosecution is able to prove the guilt of accused beyond reasonable doubts, he cannot be convicted 
by a court of law. In departmental enquiry, on the other hand, penalty can be imposed on the delinquent 
officer on a finding recorded on the basis of preponderance of probability. Procedure with respect to 
standard of proof in criminal case and departmental enquiry are different. In the case of departmental 
enquiry the technical rules of evidence have no application and the doctrine of "proof beyond doubt" has 
also no application in the departmental enquiry. Criminal prosecution is launched for an offence for 
violation of a duty the offender owes to the society or for breach of which law has provided that the offender 
shall make satisfaction to the public. So crime is an act of commission in violation of law or of omission of 
public duty. The departmental enquiry is to maintain discipline in the service and efficiency of public service. 
There would be no bar to proceed simultaneously with departmental enquiry and trial of criminal case. " 


Now looking into the evidence on record and enquiry report, the statements of the account holders, 
corroborating the charges, documents in form of deposit slips, further corroborating the statements of the depositors, 
the absence of entries with respect to deposit in the bank records also corroborating the charges, in some of the 
charges in which forging of signature has been alleged, in using the instruments for withdrawal of money, the 
handwriting has not been examined. Hence, it may be taken that these charges are not proved but remaining charges 
in which there are allegations that the workman received amounts from account holders for deposit in their accounts 
but did not deposit these amounts in the respective accounts of the account holders are held proved and finding of the 
enquiry officer as well concurrence by the competent authority with respect to proof of charges in this respect cannot 
be faulted with. With these findings, additional issue No. 1 is answered accordingly. 


Additional Issue No. 2, 


It has been submitted on behalf of workman that many workmen namely, Sanjay Satale, Ganesh Sharma, 
Shiv Ram Khrade, Dilip Patil, Mahendra Kumar Sahu, Satya Narayan who were involved in similar kinds of 
misconducts involving in amounts greater than what is alleged against the workman were awarded lesser punishment 
by appellate authority. Hence, the present workman deserves parity. 


It is further the case of the workman that these workmen were also dismissed from services by competent 
authority but their punishment was changed from dismissal to compulsory retirement by the appellate authority. 


Learned Counsel for Bank has opposed this argument. No doubt, the charges proved are acts of moral 
turpitude, they relates to lack of honesty and integrity on the part of workman, award of punishment is within the 
domain of the appointing authority and appellate authority and until and unless it is shown that punishment is 
shockingly disproportionate to the charges proved, there is no occasion for this Tribunal to interfere. 


Following cases have been referred to in this respect. 


Hon’ble Apex Court in B.C. Chaturvedi v. Union of India, (1995) 6 SCC 749 while discussing 
about the scope of judicial review, in disciplinary matters, has observed as under: 


“The High CourtTribunal, while exercising the power of judicial review, cannot normally 
substitute its own conclusion on penalty and impose some other penalty. If the punishment imposed by the

disciplinary authority or the appellate authority shocks the conscience of the High Court/Tribunal, it 
would appropriately mold the relief, either directing the disciplinary/appellate authority to reconsider the 
penalty imposed, or to shorten the litigation, it may itself, in exceptional and rare cases, imposed 
appropriate punishment with cogent reasons in support thereof.” 


In DG, RPF vs. Sai Babu (2003) 4 SCC 331, Hon’ble Apex Court has observed that: 


"Oovecacesssiers Normally, the punishment imposed by a disciplinary authority should not be 
disturbed by the High Court or a tribunal except in appropriate cases that too only after reaching a 
conclusion that the punishment imposed is grossly or shockingly disproportionate, after examining all the 
relevant factors including the nature of charges proved against, the past conduct, penalty imposed earlier, 
the nature of duties assigned having due regard to their sensitiveness, exactness expected of an discipline 
required to be maintained, and the department/establishment which the delinquent person concerned 
works.” 


In United Commercial Bank vs. P.C. Kakkar (2003) 4 SCC 364 Hon’ble Apex Court on review of 
a long line of cases and the principles of judicial review of administrative action under English law 
summarized the legal position in the following words: 


“11, The common thread running through in all these decisions is that the court should not 
interfere with the administrators’ decision unless it was illogical or suffers from procedural impropriety or 
was shocking to the conscience of the court, in the sense that it was in defiance of logic or moral 
standards. In view of what has been stated in Wednesbury case the court would not go into the 
correctness of the choice made by the administrator open to him and the court should not substitute its 
decision to that of the administrator. The scope of judicial review is judicial review is limited to the 
deficiency in decision-making process and not the decision. 


12. To put it differently, unless the punishment imposed by the disciplinary authority or the 
appellate authority shocks the conscience of the court/tribunal, there is no scope for interference. 
Further, to shorten litigation it may, in exceptional and rare cases, impose appropriate punishment by 
recording cogent reasons in support thereof.” 


In Union of India vs. S.S. Ahluwalia (2007) 7 SCC 257 Hon’ble Supreme Court reiterated the legal 
position as follows: 


“Os. 5४४४४ नर The scope of judicial review in the matter of imposition of penalty as a result of 
disciplinary proceedings is very limited. The court can interfere with the punishment only if it finds the 
same to be shockingly disproportionate to the charges found to be proved.” 


In State of Meghalaya v. Mecken Singh N. Marak (2008) 7 SCC 580 Hon’ble Supreme Court 
stated that: 


“The punishment imposed by the disciplinary authority or the appellate authority unless 
shocking to the conscience of the court, cannot be subjected to judicial review. 


Hon’ble Apex Court in Administrator, UnionTerritory of Dadra and Nagar Haveli vs. Gulbhia M. 
Lad (2010) 2 SCC (L&S) 101 has observed that 


“The legal position is fairly well settled that while exercising the power of judicial review, the 
High Court or a Tribunal cannot interfere with the discretion exercised by the disciplinary authority, 
and/or on appeal the appellate authority with regard to the imposition of punishment unless such 
discretion suffers from illegality or material procedural irregularity or that would shock the conscience of 
the court/tribunal. The exercise of discretion in imposition of punishment by the disciplinary authority or 
appellate authority is dependent on host of factors such as gravity of misconduct, past conduct, the nature 
of duties assigned to the delinquent, responsibility of the position that the delinquent holds, previous 
penalty, if any, and the discipline required to be maintained in the department or establishment he works. 
Ordinarily the court or the tribunal would not substitute its opinion on reappraisal of facts. 


This extract is taken from State Bank of Bikaner & Jaipur v. Nemi Chand Nalwaya, (2011) 4 
SCC 584: (2011) 1 SCC (L&S) 721 : 2011 SCC OnLine SC 416 at page 587 


7. It is now well settled that the courts will not act as an appellate court and reassess the evidence 
led in the domestic enquiry, nor interfere on the ground that another view is possible on the material on 
record. If the enquiry has been fairly and properly held and the findings are based on evidence, the 
question of adequacy of the evidence or the reliable nature of the evidence will not be grounds for 
interfering with the findings in departmental enquiries. Therefore, courts will not interfere with findings 
of fact recorded in departmental enquiries, except where such findings are based on no evidence or where 
they are clearly perverse. The test to find out perversity is to see whether a tribunal acting reasonably

could have arrived at such conclusion or finding, on the material on record. The courts will however 
interfere with the findings in disciplinary matters, if principles of natural justice or statutory regulations 
have been violated or if the order is found to be arbitrary, capricious, mala fide or based on extraneous 
considerations. (Vide B.C. Chaturvedi v. Union of India [(1995) 6 SCC 749 : 1996 SCC (L&S) 80 : (1996) 
32 ATC 44] , Union of India v. G. Ganayutham [(1997) 7 SCC 463 : 1997 SCC (L&S) 1806] , Bank of 
India v. Degala Suryanarayana [(1999) 5 SCC 762 : 1999 SCC (L&S) 1036] and High Court of 
Judicature at Bombay v. Shashikant S. Patil [(2000) 1 SCC 416 : 2000 SCC (L&S) 144] .) 


In Air India Corporation Bombay vs. V.A. Ravellow 1972 (25) FLR 319 (SC) it has been observed 
that: 


“Once the employer has lost the confidence in the employee and the bona fide loss of confidence 
is affirmed, the order of punishment must be considered to be immune from challenge, for the reason that 
discharging the office of trust and confidence requires absolute integrity, and in a case of loss of 
confidence, reinstatement cannot be directed.” 


In Knhaiyalal Agarwal and others vs. Factory Manager, Gwaliar Sugar Co. Ltd. AIR 2001 SC 
3645 Hon’ble Apex Court laid down the test for loss of confidence to find out as to whether there was bona 
fide loss of confidence in the employee, observing that: 


“Loss of confidence cannot be subjective, based upon the mind of the management. Objective 
facts which would lead to a definite inference of apprehension in the mind of the management, regarding 
trust worthiness or reliability of the employee, must be alleged and proved.” 


The only ground remains now is that of parity, in my considered view the disciplinary authority took a very 
lenient way with respect to the workman, these punishments were altered. Only this ground is not sufficient to 
interfere with the punishment of the workman, in the case in hand, the misconducts proved are series of acts 
involving lack of integrity and honesty and acts of moral turpitude. I find the punishment not so disproportionate 
to the charges proved to warrant interference and also not a fit case to grant parity. 


Additional issue No. 2 stands answered accordingly. 
In light of above discussion and findings, the reference is answered as follows.- 
AWARD 


Holding the action of the management of Narmada Jhabua Gramin Bank in terminating the service of 
workman Shri Shankar Singh Bamaniya w.e.f. 07.10.2014, is legal, proper and justified, he is held entitled to 
no relief.”

As per letter dated 01/09/2015 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 


made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification No. L- 
12011/41/2015-(IR(B-D) dt. 01/09/2015. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“क्या AHAT राष्ट्रीयक्ृत बैंक कर्मचारी संगठन TART At बन्रवंत Rig Ms की स्टेट बैंक ऑफ SAT TART

न्यायोचित हैं? यवि हां तो प्रार्थी किस अनुतोष का भागी EP?” 


Notices were issued to both the parties. They appeared and filed their respective statement of claim and 
defense. 

The undisputed facts are mainly that, the workman Balwant Singh Gaud was dismissed by the Bank for 
misconduct which was found proved against him after a departmental enquiry. This dismissal was effective from 
03.04.2010. The Workman raised a dispute in this respect. A reference case No. R/103/2012 proceeded before this 
Tribunal and is pending disposal according to the Management. The workman alleges that after dismissal, the 
Management did not pay him the employer’s contribution which the Management contributed towards his Provident 
Fund which is unjust, illegal and arbitrary on the part of the Management. 

The case of the Management is that according to the Circular No. PA/CIR/27 dated 11.02.1985 and 
Circular No. PA/CIR/137 dated 23.09.1986 when a employee is dismissed from the service the Bank’s Contribution 
to his provident fund shall not be payable to him. Bank has also pleaded that, payment of employees contribution 
shall be subject to the final order in the reference case which is against dismissal of the Workman. 

The Workman side has filed photocopy documents admitted by Management which are Exhibit W-1 to W- 
6 to be referred to as and when require. 

I have heard argument of Learned Counsel Mr. Arun Patel for Workman. Learned Counsel for Management 
was not available. I have gone through the record. 

In the light of the aforesaid circular which provides that Banks contribution to Provident Fund of an 
Employee will not be paid to him on his dismissal, the Management of Bank is held justified in not paying the 
Banks Contribution to the Provident Fund amount of the Workman till his dismissal is set-aside by a 
Competent Forum. 

The reference stands answered accordingly. 

No order as to cost.

Section 25 (T & U) of the Act is reproduced as follows:- 


251. Prohibition of unfair labour practice —No employer or workman or a trade union, whether registered under 
the Trade Unions Act, 1926 (18 of 1926), or not, shall commit any unfair labour practice. 


25U. Penalty for committing unfair labour practices—Any person who commits any unfair labour practice shall 
be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months or with fine which may extend to one

From perusal of Schedule and provisions mentioned above, Act of engaging contract labours, casual or 
temporaries and to continue them as such for years with the object of depriving them of status, privileges of 
permanent workman is unfair labour practice adopted by management which have been prohibited under section 25-T 
of the Act, section 25-U of the Act provides penal consequences for such an unfair labour practice too. 


The Act may have civil and penal consequences both. Same is the case with unfair labour practice, the penal 
consequences of unfair labour practice is provided in the Act but civil consequences are not provided. This fact does 
not denude the Courts and Tribunals under the Act to undo the effects of such Act like unfair labour practice which is 
prohibited by the Act.

16. The respondent Corporation has neither produced documentary evidence nor showed before the Labour 
Court that the appellant workman was appointed on contract basis. The fact that he deposited Rs 2000 towards 
security amount with the respondent Corporation indicates that he was working as a driver on a permanent basis. In 
view of Schedule V, Item 10 of the ID Act, 1947 the respondent Corporation is prohibited from engaging the appellant 
workman as a badli, casual or temporary workman to work on permanent basis. The fact that he had been 
continuously working for more than 3 years and he had rendered more than 240 days of service as the driver in a 
calendar year until his termination order and yet he is being engaged on a contractual basis in the respondent 
Corporation is statutorily prohibited. The same amounts to an unfair labour practice as defined under Section 2(ra) 
read with Section 25-T, which action of the Corporation is punishable under Section 25-U of the ID Act. This legal 
position is settled by this Court in Chief Conservator of Forests case [Chief Conservator of Forests v. Jagannath 
Maruti Kondhare, (1996) 2 SCC 293 : 1996 SCC (L&S) 500] wherein it was held as under : (SCC pp. 302-03, para 
22) 


“22. ... In our opinion, it would be permissible on facts of a particular case to draw the inference mentioned 
in the second part of the item, if badlis, casuals or temporaries are continued as such for years. We further state 
that the present was such a case inasmuch as from the materials on record we are satisfied that the 25 workmen 
who went to the Industrial Court of Pune (and 15 to the Industrial Court, Ahmednagar) had been kept as casuals 
for long years with the primary object of depriving them of the status of permanent employees inasmuch as giving 
of this status would have required the employer to pay the workmen at a rate higher than the one fixed under the 
Minimum Wages Act. We can think of no other possible object as, it may be remembered, that the Pachgaon 
Parwati Scheme was intended to cater to the recreational and educational aspirations also of the populace, 
which are not ephemeral objects, but par excellence permanent. We would say the same about environment- 
pollution-care work of Ahmednagar, whose need is on the increase because of increase in pollution. Permanency 
is thus writ large on the face of both the types of work. If, even in such projects, persons are kept in jobs on 
casual basis for years the object manifests itself; no scrutiny is required. We, therefore, answer the second 
question also against the appellants.”

“36. ... ‘22. The Industrial Disputes Act is a benign measure which seeks to pre-empt industrial tensions, 
provide the mechanics of dispute resolutions and set up the necessary infrastructure, so that the energies of the 
partners in production may not be dissipated in counterproductive battles and the assurance of industrial justice 
may create a climate of goodwill.’ (D.J. Bahadur case [(1981) I SCC 315 : 1981 SCC (L&S) 111 : (1981) 1 SCR 
1083] , SCC p. 334, per Krishna Iyer, J.) 


In order to achieve the aforesaid objectives, the Labour Courts/Industrial Tribunals are given wide powers not 
only to enforce the rights but even to create new rights, with the underlying objective to achieve social justice. 
Way back in the year 1950 i.e. immediately after the enactment of the Industrial Disputes Act, in one of its first 
and celebrated judgment in Bharat Bank Ltd. v. Employees [1950 SCC 470 : AIR 1950 SC 188 : 1950 LLJ 921 at 
p. 948] this aspect was highlighted by the Court observing as under : (AIR p. 209, para 61) 


‘61. ... In settling the disputes between the employers and the workmen, the function of the Tribunal is 
not confined to administration of justice in accordance with law. It can confer rights and privileges on either 
party which it considers reasonable and proper, though they may not be within the terms of any existing 
agreement. It has not merely to interpret or give effect to the contractual rights and obligations of the 
parties. It can create new rights and obligations between them which it considers essential for keeping 
industrial peace.’” 


25.3. And again at para 37, observing that the aforesaid sweeping power conferred upon the Tribunal is not 
unbridled and is circumscribed by this Court in New Maneck Chowk Spg. & Wvg. Co. Ltd. v. Textile Labour 
Assn. [AIR 1961 SC 867] , the relevant para 6 of which is extracted as under : (Hari Nandan Prasad case [Hari 
Nandan Prasad v. Food Corporation of India, (2014) 7 SCC 190 : (2014) 2 SCC (L&S) 408] , SCC p. 213, paras 37- 
38) 


“37. ... 6. ... This, however, does not mean that an Industrial Court can do anything and everything when 
dealing with an industrial dispute. This power is conditioned by the subject-matter with which it is dealing and 
also by the existing industrial law and it would not be open to it while dealing with a particular matter before it 
to overlook the industrial law relating to that matter as laid down by the legislature or by this Court.’ (Textile 
Labour Assn. case [AIR 1961 SC 867] , AIR p. 870) 


38. It is, thus, this fine balancing which is required to be achieved while adjudicating a particular dispute, 
keeping in mind that the industrial disputes are settled by industrial adjudication on principle of fair play and 
justice.” 


26. In view of the aforesaid statement of law laid down by this Court after adverting to the powers of the 
Industrial Tribunal and the Labour Court as interpreted by this Court in the earlier decisions referred to supra, the 
said principle is aptly applicable to the fact situation of the case on hand, for the reason that the Labour Court 
recorded a finding of fact in favour of the workman that the termination of services of the appellant herein is not legal 
and valid and further reaffirmed the said finding and also clearly held that the plea taken in the order of termination 
that he was appointed on contract basis as a driver is not proved by producing cogent evidence. Further, we hold that 
even if the plea of the employer is accepted, extracting work though of permanent nature continuously for more than 
three years, the alleged employment on contract basis is wholly impermissible. Therefore, we have held that it 
amounts to an unfair labour practice as defined under Section 2(ra) of the ID Act, 1947 read with Section 25-T which 
is prohibited under Section 25-U, Chapter V-C of the ID Act, 1947. We have to hold that the judgment of the High 
Court in reversing the award is not legal and the same is set aside by us.

thus : (SCC p. 205, para 21) 


“21. Before concluding, we consider it necessary to observe that while exercising jurisdiction under Articles 
226 and/or 227 of the Constitution in matters like the present one, the High Courts are duty-bound to keep in 
mind that the Industrial Disputes Act and other similar legislative instruments are social welfare legislations and 
the same are required to be interpreted keeping in view the goals set out in the Preamble of the Constitution and 
the provisions contained in Part IV thereof in general and Articles 38, 39(a) to (e), 43 and 43-A in particular, 
which mandate that the State should secure a social order for the promotion of welfare of the people, ensure 
equality between men and women and equitable distribution of material resources of the community to subserve 
the common good and also ensure that the workers get their dues. More than 41 years ago, Gajendragadkar, J. 
opined that: 


‘10. ... the concept of social and economic justice is a living concept of revolutionary import; it gives 
sustenance to the rule of law and meaning and significance to the ideal of welfare State.’ 


(State of Mysore v. Workers of Gold Mines [AIR 1958 SC 923] , AIR p. 928, para 10.)” 


24. We are of the opinion that the view taken in Maharashtra SRTC [Maharashtra SRTC v. Casteribe Rajya 
Parivahan Karmchari Sanghatana, (2009) 8 SCC 556 : (2009) 2 SCC (L&S) 513] at para 36 after 
distinguishing Umadevi (3) case [State of Karnataka v. Umadevi (3), (2006) 4 SCC 1 : 2006 SCC (L&S) 753] is the 
plausible view. Therefore, we have to hold that the finding of the High Court in setting aside the finding of fact 
recorded by the Labour Court in its award by applying Umadevi (3) case [State of Karnataka v. Umadevi (3), (2006) 
4 SCC 1 : 2006 SCC (L&S) 753] is wholly untenable in law. Therefore, the same is set aside by this Court. 


23. Further, the reliance placed upon the decision of this Court on Umadevi (3) case [State of 
Karnataka v. Umadevi (3), (2006) 4 SCC 7 : 2006 SCC (L&S) 753] by the High Court to reverse the finding of fact 
recorded in the award in favour of the workman in answering the points of dispute in the negative, is not tenable in 
law in view of the judgment of this Court in Maharashtra SRTC v. Casteribe Rajya Parivahan Karmchari 
Sanghatana [Maharashtra SRTC v. Casteribe Rajya Parivahan Karmchari Sanghatana, (2009) 8 SCC 556 : (2009) 2 
SCC (L&S) 513] , wherein, this Court after adverting to Umadevi (3) case [State of Karnataka v. Umadevi (3), (2006) 
4 SCC I : 2006 SCC (L&S) 753] at para 36, has held that the said case does not denude the Industrial and Labour 
Courts of their statutory power under Section 30 read with Section 32 of the MRTU and PULP Act to order 
permanency of the workers who have been victims of unfair labour practice on the part of the employer under Item 6 
of Schedule IV where the posts on which they have been working exist”. (SCC p. 574) 


Further, this Court held that : (SCC p. 574, para 36) 


“36. ... Umadevi (3) case [State of Karnataka v. Umadevi (3), (2006) 4 SCC 7 : 2006 SCC (L&S) 753] 
cannot be held to have overridden the powers of the Industrial and Labour Courts in passing appropriate order 
under Section 30 of the MRTU and PULP Act, once unfair labour practice on the part of the employer under Item 
6 of Schedule IV is established.” 


It is not disputed that these workmen have been working though the Contractors have changed intermittently 
every year. It is also not disputed that the job still exists and is being done by these workmen since 1999 till date, 
which establishes that this job is of permanent and perennial nature. 


By not employing workmen on permanent regular basis against the permanent vacancy and engaging 
contract labours for a work of permanent perennial nature either directly or by outsourcing agencies, the management 
is held adopting unfair labour practice which is prohibited under the Act. 


As mentioned above, engaging Badli or contract workers by management and continue with contract workers 
for a long time is Unfair Labour Practice. Hence even if, it be taken that the applicant/workers are outsourcing 
employees, the management in this case is held to have adopted Unfair Labour Practice by engaging them as contract 
labours since 1999 till date and it will make no difference that whether they have been supplied by the security 
agencies as outsourced employee or have been directly engaged by the Management Corporation, in both the cases 
they are contract workers. 


It is settled proposition of law that this Tribunal within its power to lift the veil and look into the facts in 
order to determine the facts whether the contract said to have entered into by the management and outsourcing 
agencies is sham or camouflage or not. 


In light of the establish facts that the applicant/workmen have been working since 1999 till date, hence, the 
work is of permanent and perennial nature, only the contractors have changed and not the workmen in these years and 
also that these workmen have been working at a site of Management Corporation under their directions makes its 
sufficiently clear that infact, the outsourcing contracts are sham and bogus, rather they are a camouflage to deny the 
applicant/workmen, their legally admissible dues. 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7081 


In light of the above discussion and finding the question rises as to what relief, workmen are entitled to? 


Reference may be taken of judgment of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Jaggo v/s Union of India 
reported in (2024) SCC Online SC 3826 , the relevant paragraphs of this judgment are being reproduced as follows:- 


“22. The pervasive misuse of temporary employment contracts, as exemplified in this case, reflects a broader 
systemic issue that adversely affects workers’ rights and job security. In the private sector, the rise of the gig economy 
has led to an increase in precarious employment arrangements, often characterized by lack of benefits, job security, 
and fair treatment. Such practices have been criticized for exploiting workers and undermining labour standards. 
Government institutions, entrusted with upholding the principles of fairness and justice, bear an even greater 
responsibility to avoid such exploitative employment practices. When public sector entities engage in misuse of 
temporary contracts, it not only mirrors the detrimental trends observed in the gig economy but also sets a 
concerning precedent that can erode public trust in governmental operations. 


25. It is a disconcerting reality that temporary employees, particularly in government institutions, often face 
multifaceted forms of exploitation. While the foundational purpose of temporary contracts may have been to address 
short-term or seasonal needs, they have increasingly become a mechanism to evade long-term obligations owed to 
employees. These practices manifest in several ways: 


¢ Misuse of “Temporary” Labels:- Employees engaged for work that is essential, recurring, and integral to 
the functioning of an institution are often labelled as “temporary” or “contractual,” even when their roles mirror 
those of regular employees. Such misclassification deprives workers of the dignity, security, and benefits that regular 
employees are entitled to, despite performing identical tasks. 


5 Arbitrary Termination:- Temporary employees are frequently dismissed without cause or notice, as seen in 
the present case. This practice undermines the principles of natural justice and subjects workers to a state of constant 
insecurity, regardless of the quality or duration of their service. 


¢ Lack of Career Progression:- Temporary employees often find themselves excluded from opportunities for 
skill development, promotions, or incremental pay raises. They remain stagnant in their roles, creating a systemic 
disparity between them and their regular counterparts, despite their contributions being equally significant. 


¢ Using Outsourcing as_a Shield:- Institutions increasingly resort to outsourcing roles performed by 
temporary employees, effectively replacing one set of exploited workers with another. This practice not only 
perpetuates exploitation but also demonstrates a deliberate effort to bypass the obligation to offer regular 
employment. 


¢ Denial of Basic Rights and Benefits:- Temporary employees are often denied fundamental benefits such as 
pension, provident fund, health insurance, and paid leave, even when their tenure spans decades. This lack of social 
security subjects them and their families to undue hardship, especially in cases of illness, retirement, or unforeseen 
circumstances.” 


The principle laid down in the case of Jaggo (Supra) has been followed by Hon’ble Supreme Court in the 
case of Shripal Vs. Nagar Nigam Ghaziabad in Civil Appeal No. 8157/2024 (2025 INSC 144). The relevant portion of 
the said judgment is being reproduced as follows:- 


“12. The evidence, including documentary material and undisputed facts, reveals that the Appellant 
Workmen performed duties integral to the Respondent Employer’s municipal functions specifically the upkeep of 
parks, horticultural tasks, and city beautification efforts. Such work is evidently perennial rather than sporadic or 
project-based. Reliance on a general “ban on fresh recruitment” cannot be used to deny labor protections to long 
serving workmen. On the contrary, the acknowledged shortage of Gardeners in the Ghaziabad Nagar Nigam 
reinforces the notion that these positions are essential and ongoing, not intermittent. By requiring the same tasks 
(planting, pruning, general upkeep) from the Appellant Workmen as from regular Gardeners but still compensating 
them inadequately and inconsistently the Respondent Employer has effectively engaged in an unfair labour practice. 
The principle of “equal pay for equal work,” repeatedly emphasized by this Court, cannot be casually disregarded 
when workers have served for extended periods in roles resembling those of permanent employees. Long-standing 
assignments under the Employer's direct supervision belie any notion that these were mere short-term casual 
engagements. 


14, The Respondent Employer places reliance on Umadevi (supra) to contend that daily-wage or temporary 
employees cannot claim permanent absorption in the absence of statutory rules providing such absorption. However, 
as frequently reiterated, Uma Devi itself distinguishes between appointments that are “illegal” and those that are 
“irregular,” the latter being eligible for regularization if they meet certain conditions. More importantly, Uma Devi 
cannot serve as a Shield to justify exploitative engagements persisting for years without the Employer undertaking 
legitimate recruitment. Given the record which shows no true contractor based arrangement and a consistent need 
for permanent horticultural staff the alleged asserted ban on fresh recruitment, though real, cannot justify indefinite 
daily-wage status or continued unfair practices. 


7082 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


15. It is manifest that the Appellant Workmen continuously rendered their services over several years, 
sometimes spanning more than a decade. Even if certain muster rolls were not produced in full, the Employer’s 
failure to furnish such records—despite directions to do so—allows an adverse inference under well-established 
labour jurisprudence. Indian labour law strongly disfavors perpetual daily-wage or contractual engagements in 
circumstances where the work is permanent in nature. Morally and legally, workers who fulfil ongoing municipal 
requirements year after year cannot be dismissed summarily as dispensable, particularly in the absence of a genuine 
contractor agreement. At this juncture, it would be appropriate to recall the broader critique of indefinite 
“temporary” employment practices as done by a recent judgement of this court in Jaggo v. Union of India 


16. The High Court did acknowledge the Employer’s inability to justify these abrupt terminations. 
Consequently, it ordered re-engagement on daily wages with some measure of parity in minimum pay. Regrettably, 
this only perpetuated precariousness: the Appellant Workmen were left in a marginally improved yet still uncertain 
status. While the High Court recognized the importance of their work and hinted at eventual regularization, it failed 
to afford them continuity of service or meaningful back wages commensurate with the degree of statutory violation 
evident on record. 


17. In light of these considerations, the Employer’s discontinuation of the Appellant Workmen stands in 
violation of the most basic labour law principles. Once it is established that their services were terminated without 
adhering to Sections 6E and 6N of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and that they were engaged in essential, 
perennial duties, these workers cannot be relegated to perpetual uncertainty. While concerns of municipal budget and 
compliance with recruitment rules merit consideration, such concerns do not absolve the Employer of statutory 
obligations or negate equitable entitlements. Indeed, bureaucratic limitations cannot trump the legitimate rights of 
workmen who have served continuously in de facto regular roles for an extended period. 18. The impugned order of 
the High Court, to the extent they confine the Appellant Workmen to future daily-wage engagement without continuity 
or meaningful back wages, is hereby set aside with the following directions: - 


I. The discontinuation of the Appellant Workmen’s services, effected without compliance with Section 6E 
and Section 6N of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, is declared illegal. All orders or communications 
terminating their services are quashed. In consequence, the Appellant Workmen shall be treated as continuing in 
service from thereof their termination, for all purposes, including seniority and continuity in service. 


II. The Respondent Employer shall reinstate the Appellant Workmen in their respective posts (or posts akin 
to the duties they previously performed) within four weeks from the date of this judgment. Their entire period of 
absence (from the date of termination until actual reinstatement) shall be counted for continuity of service and all 
consequential benefits, such as seniority and eligibility for promotions, if any. 


III. Considering the length of service, the Appellant Workmen shall be entitled to 50% of the back wages 
from the date of their discontinuation until their actual reinstatement. The Respondent Employer shall clear the 
aforesaid dues within three months from the date of their reinstatement. 


IV. The Respondent Employer is directed to initiate a fair and transparent process for regularizing the 
Appellant Workmen within six months from the date of reinstatement, duly considering the fact that they have 
performed perennial municipal duties akin to permanent posts. In assessing regularization, the Employer shall not 
impose educational or procedural criteria retroactively if such requirements were never applied to the Appellant 
Workmen or to similarly situated regular employees in the past. To the extent that sanctioned vacancies for such 
duties exist or are required, the Respondent Employer shall expedite all necessary administrative processes to ensure 
these longtime employees are not indefinitely retained on contract labour contrary to statutory and equitable norms.” 


On the basis of above discussion and findings, the reference deserves to be answered as follows:- 
AWARD 


Holding the action of the management of Cement Corporation of India, Nayagaon Cement Factory, 
Neemuch in not regularizing the service of Shri Gheesalal Sharma S/o Ramnivas Sharma & 38 others even after 
completing 240 days in a calendar year, unjustified in law. The management of Cement Corporation of India is 
directed to initiate a fair and transparent process for regularizing the Appellant Workmen within six months from 
the date of publication of award, duly considering the fact that these workmen have performed perennial duties as 
security guards akin to permanent security guards of the Management Corporation. In assessing regularization, 
the Employer shall not impose educational or procedural criteria retroactively if such requirements were never 
applied to the Appellant Workmen or to similarly situated regular employees in the past. To the extent that 
sanctioned vacancies for such duties exist or are required, the Respondent Employer shall expedite all necessary 
administrative processes to ensure these longtime employees are not indefinitely retained as contract labour 
contrary to statutory and equitable norms. 


No order as to cost.

As per letter dated 21/03/2017 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification No. L- 
26012/10/2016-(IR(M)) dt. 21/03/2017. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the action of Management in terminating the services of Shri Girdhari Sahu S/o Late Prahlad 
Sahu, Ex-Attendant, working in public Health Engg. Department of Bhilai Steel Plant on the ground of 
absenteeism and communicated through order T&/PHED/H/2015/288 dated 29-01-2015 is legal and 
justified? If not, what relief the workman is entitled to?” 


7084 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


Notices were issued to both the parties. They appeared and filed their respective statement of claim and 
defense. 


Case of the Workman is that he was initially appointed in 2009 on the post of Attendant in Public Health 
Engineering Department of Management. He was terminated vide order of Management dated 29.01.2015 for the 
charge of unauthorized absence from his Workplace since March 2012 to May 2013. According to Workman, no full 
and proper opportunity was given to defend his case. It is also alleged that the charges have been wrongly held proved 
and the punishment is disproportionate to the charge. 


Case of the Management on this issue is that, the Workman was working as Attendant since 01.11.2009 he 
was habitual absentee, he had history of unauthorized absenteeism in which he was punished as many as three times 
but he did not improved. For the present charge, he admitted the charge during the enquiry. He was issued a show- 
cause notice on Enquiry Report before Awarding punishment. 


Management has filed photocopy enquiry papers which have been admitted by Workman. 
According to Management the charges have been accordingly held proved and the punishment is also 
proportionate to the misconduct proved. 
Following preliminary issues was framed on the basis of pleadings. 
1. Whether the Departmental Enquiry conducted against the Workman is legal? 
This issue was decided on the basis of evidence vide order dated 13.02.2025 holding the Departmental 
Enquiry legal and proper. This order is part of this Judgment. 
Following additional issues were framed thereafter — 
1. Whether the charges are proved? 
2. Whether the punishment is proportionate to the charge? 


Parties were given opportunity to lead evidences if any on these issues. No evidences were filed by any of 
the parties. I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for Workman Mr. Arun Patel and Learned Counsel Mr. R.C. 
Shrivastava for the Management. I have gone through the record as well. 


Additional Issue No. 1 — 


The settled preposition of law with respect to proof of charges in Departmental proceeding is that, the 
charges need not be proved beyond doubt as it is required in Criminal Trials, they are required to be proved to the 
extent of probability and possibility only. Now looking into the evidences collected during the enquiry, it comes out 
that, the absence of the Workman is not disputed during the enquiry. 


Case of the Workman is that, he was getting treatment on different station for some skin disease hence he 
could not inform the Management and could not attend his job. There is nothing on record in the enquiry papers to 
show that any document or any certificate by the Doctor had been produced during the enquiry or even before this 
Tribunal to show that during the period of absence in the charge sheet, the Workman was confined to bed and was 
advised bed rest. In absence of such evidence, the enquiry officer and competent authority cannot be held unjustified 
in recording finding that the absence of the Workman was willful, and unauthorized. Hence, the charges are held 
proved against the Workman. 


Additional Issue No.1 is answered accordingly. 
Additional Issue No.2 - 


On the basis of evidence during the enquiry, it comes that, workman has been in the habit of willful and 
unauthorizedly absenting himself from workplace in earlier years also and he was punished for this misconduct earlier 
also thrice in 2011, and once in 2012 & 2013. Keeping in view the fact that, he is a repeated offender, the punishment 
ordered is held not so disproportionate to shock the conscious of this Tribunal. Hence, holding the punishment not 
disproportionate to the charges to warrant interference this additional issue is answered accordingly. 


On the basis of above discussion and findings the reference is answered as follows. 
AWARD 


Holding the action of Management in terminating the services of Shri Girdhari Sahu S/o Late Prahlad 
Sahu, Ex-Attendant, working in public Health Engg. Department of Bhilai Steel Plant is not against law. He is 
entitled to no relief. 


No order as to cost.

As per letter dated 11/08/2014 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference 
has been made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per 
Notification No. L-29012/9/2014-IR (M) dt. 11/08/2014. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the action of the management of Bhilai Steel Plant, Iron Ore Complex, Dalli Rajhara, Distt- 
Balod in not correcting the date of birth of Sh. G. Satyam, Staff Attendant, (Personnel No. 990002) from 
05.07.1954 to 27.05.1959 is justified or not? If not, what relief the workman is entitled to?” 


After registering the case on the basis of reference, notices were issued to the parties. They appeared and 
filed their respective statement of claim in defense. 


Case of the applicant/Workman is mainly that he was first appointed as Head Cook in the statutory 
Canteen of the management company from 01.05.1978, his date of birth was recorded as 27.05.1959. On his 
regularization as Staff Attendant, he was posted as Staff Attendant in the Mines Organization of the management vide 
order dated 26.11.2009 in the Rajhara Mines, his date of birth was recorded in Form-B maintained by the Mines as 
27.05.1959 and was attested by Mines Manager, he had submitted his attestation Form dated 07.11.2009 containing 
his same date of birth i.e., 27.05.1959, attested by the Deputy General Manager (Mines), he had obtained his school 
leaving certificate dated 23.04.1966 from the school where he was first admitted. His same date of birth i.e., 
27.05.1959 was recorded in the certificate. The management arbitrarily changed his date of birth from 27.05.1959 to 
05.07.1954 in their record. He filed written representation on 08.09.2011 requesting the management to correct his 
date of birth as the mistake was detected by him only in the year 2011 but of no avail. He again filed a detailed 
representation on 08.05.2013 to the Chief Executive Officer, the General Manager Rajhara Mines and the General 
Manager (Personnel) through proper channel. This representation was also not heard of and no action was taken. He 
raised dispute in this respect before the Assistant Labour Commissioner, the Union also raised the dispute in this 
respect after failure of conciliation, the reference was made to this Tribunal. 


In the meanwhile, the management superannuated him on the basis of his incorrect date of birth 05.07.1954. 
According to the workman, the action of changing date of birth of the workman by the management is unjust, illegal, 
malafide and arbitrary. Subsequently, the action of management in superannuating him on the basis of his changed 
date of birth is also arbitrary and illegal. The workman has requested that holding the action of management in 
unilaterally changing his date of birth from 27.05.1959 to 05.07.1954, unjust, illegal and arbitrary, the action of 
management in superannuating the workman on the basis of changed date of birth 05.07.1954 be held unjust, illegal 
and arbitrary. Further, he be held entitled to be reinstated and entitled to all consequential pre as well post retiral 
benefits, deeming him in service till the date of his superannuation based on his date of birth 27.05.1959. 


The case of the management is mainly that, the workman was appointed as Head Cook on 01.05.1978 by 
Employees New Cooperative Canteen. Subsequently, he was appointed as Attendant in Bhilai Steel Plant in grade S-1 
vide offer letter dated 28.10.2009, he joined on 01.11.2009. He was placed in Rajhara Mines on 05.12.2009, in 
connection with order of Hon’ble High Court of M.P., Jabalpur in L.P.A. No. 208 & 209 of 1995 a detail information 
was collected from all the cooperative canteens in the year 1996. The President, Coke Oven Cooperative Society

Canteen submitted list of canteen workers working in the Coke Oven Cooperative Canteen in the prescribed format 
showing the date of birth of the workman as 05.07.1954. On the basis of this list, the canteen workers in the list were 
subjected to medical examination, the date of birth of the workman was mentioned as 05.07.1954 in the medical 
examination, based on declaration made by him. The workman submitted declaration Form with respect to dependant 
family members for free medical treatment in which he had declared his age as 56 years on 17.11.2011 which nears to 
1954, he put his signature on that Form. 


It is further the case of the management that the workman did not submit any record with respect to his 
educational qualification/ date of birth, etc. The CPF declaration & nomination submitted before Coke Oven 
Cooperative Canteen by the workman prior to absorption in the Bhilai Steel Plant shows his date of birth 05.07.1954. 
The retirement age of employees working in the management is 60 years, the workman was issued retirement notice 
dated 31.05.2014 and he has been superannuated on the basis of his date of birth 05.07.1954 vide order of 
management effective from 31.07.1954. Thus according to management, Form-B Register, Service Register, 
Attestation Form, CPF declaration and nomination Form and Medical Examination Certificate mentions his date of 
birth as 05.07.1954 which he was very well aware of, he raised the dispute in this respect at fag end of its service, the 
management has thus requested that the reference be answered against the workman. 


The Workman has filed his rejoinder wherein he has stated that the so called list sent by the President does 
not bear the signature of workman, hence he is not responsible for any entry in the list which was not prepared by him 
nor was counter signed by him. He has mainly reiterated his allegation taken in his statement of claim. 


Case No. A-01/2014 has been filed by the applicant/workman under section 33-A of the Act, challenging the 
same order of management with regard to his superannuation on the basis of his date of birth 05.07.1954, on the 
ground that it is in violation of section 33-A of the Act with almost the same allegations. Management has also filed 
its written reply with almost the same pleadings taken by them in case No. R-75/2014 


Since the parties, the facts and dispute in both the cases are similar, hence vide order dated 14.12.2015 
passed by my learned predecessor, both the cases were consolidated and case No. R-75/2014 has been made 
leading case. 


In evidence, the workman has filed his affidavit as his Examination-in-chief, he has been cross-examined by 
management. 


The President of the Union has also filed his affidavit as his Examination-in-chief. He has also been cross- 
examined by management. 


The workman has filed and proved his original appointment letter dated 01.05.1978, certificate issued by the 
Manager of canteen dated 05.11.2005 CPF declaration and nomination Form dated 11.06.1999 with respect to 
Cooperative Canteen, RTI obtained document, attestation Form, Form-B prepared in Rajhara Mines, CPF declaration 
Form in Rajhara Mines, medical examination record in Rajhara Mines, documents which are representations and 
replies during conciliation proceedings before Labour Commissioner. 


Management has filed affidavit of its witness Rohit Kumar, Personnel Officer as his Examination-in-chief, 
has also filed and proved letter of Manager, P. Panigrahi canteen dated 17.05.1996, asking the President, Coke Oven 
Cooperative Society Canteen to furnish information with respect to persons employed in the canteen in compliance of 
order of Hon’ble High Court, letter of President with list, list of canteen workers for medical examination, declaration 
with respect to dependants for free treatment, CPF declaration and nomination Form. 


It is also worth mention here that, the workman died during the pendency of the proceeding, his legal 
representatives have been substituted in his place. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for the Workman Mr. Arun Patel and Mr. R. C. Shrivastava, 
Learned Counsel for the Management. I have gone through the record as well. 


On perusal of record in light of rival arguments, the reference itself is the issue for determination. 


Pleadings of the parties have already been detailed earlier, the workman side has corroborated its case, as 
stated above, in workman affidavit as his Examination-in-chief, he has stated that he was first appointed as head cook 
on 01.05.1978 his date of birth was recorded on 27.05.1959 in his service record at the time of his appointment his 
service were regularized and thereafter he was appointed as Staff Attendant w.e.f., 26.11.2009, the management 
altered his date of birth in his service record without his consent and changed it from 27.05.1959 to 05.07.1954, which 
is illegal on the part of management and has superannuated him on the basis of his changed date of birth. He has 
proved Form-B Ex-W/1 maintained by Rajhara Mines after his confirmation which bears his date of birth 27.05.1959, 
he has further proved Attestation Form prepared during his first service i.e., Coke Oven Cooperative Society where he 
was appointed as Head Cook, this form also contains his date of birth 27.05.1959, he has further filed his school 
leaving certificate and proved it as Ex-W/3 which contain his date of birth 27.05.1959. 


7088 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


He has further filed and proved various communications made by the Labour Commissioner with respect to 
his representations regarding correction of his date of birth which are Ex-W/5 to Ex-W/11. In his cross-examination 
he has stated that he studied in school till class Second regarding the document of management which is signed and 
prepared by the President of the Canteen Society which is list of the canteen workers and CPF declaration and 
nomination Form Ex-M/1 and Ex-M/2. He has stated that his signatures on these forms have not been done by him. 


The President of the workman union has also examined himself by way of filing his affidavit as his 
Examination-in-chief, he has also been examined by management. His statements corroborate the statement of the 
workman 


The management witness has corroborated the case of the management in his statement on oath as his 
Examination-in-chief, he has stated that the workman was first appointed as head cook on 01.05.1978 by Employees 
Cooperative Canteen Cook Oven, he was subsequently appointed as Attendant in Bhilai Steel Plant vide letter dated 
28.10.2009, he joined on 01.11.2009 and was posted in Rajhara Mines where he joined on 05.12.2009 under order of 
Hon’ble High Court, President of the Canteen Union submitted his recommendation containing list of employee 
workers in the canteen which contained name of the applicant/workman, also his date of birth was mentioned as 
05.07.1954 in that list. The workman mentioned his same date of birth i.e., 05.07.1954 in his declaration form 
regarding dependant family members mentioning his age as 56 years as on 17.11.2011 which corresponds to 1954 and 
put his signature, he did not submitted any document regarding his educational qualification, the CPF declaration and 
nomination submitted by him before Coke Oven Cooperative Canteen also contained his date of birth as 05.07.1954, 
he was superannuated on his date of birth 05.07.1954 after attaining 60 years of age, he was well aware regarding his 
date of birth 05.07.1954 recorded in documents maintained by the management. He could not produce any reliable 
document with regard to his date of birth 27.05.1959 as claimed by him, management witness has proved these 
documents mentioned above.. 


On the basis of comparative analysis of the documentary as well statements on behalf of the parties, it comes 
out that undisputedly, the date of birth of the workman where he was first employed was recorded as 27.05.1959. The 
same date of birth was recorded in Form-B at Rajhara Mines after his regularization. The Attestation Form filed by 
him while he was posted in Rajhara Mines, also contains the same date of birth 27.05.1959, his school leaving 
certificate also contains the same date of birth. In his first document regarding his appointment, he has made his 
signature, hence he cannot be said to be illiterate. The first document containing his changed date of birth as 
01.05.1954 is the list of employees prepared by the Coke Oven Cooperative Society Canteen, this list was not 
prepared by the workman, hence he cannot be held responsible for any entry regarding the date of birth in the list 
since the person who prepared the list and filed has not been examined by management, it cannot be said that on what 
basis he mentioned date of birth of the workman as 01.05.1954 whereas at that time the service records of the 
workman contained his date of birth as 27.05.1959. Thereafter, in Form-B Register maintained by management, 
Service Register, Attestation Form, CPF declaration and nomination Form his date of birth 05.07.1954 is mentioned, 
the medical declaration form does not contain date of birth of the workman rather it contain his approximate age at 
time of filling form i.e., 17.11.2011, the CPF declaration and nomination Form Ex-M/1 does not contain the signature 
of the workman, there is overwriting in the column of date of birth which has been prepared on 01.06.1990. 


It is apparent from the date mentioned on it, the CPF declaration and nomination Form filed and proved by 
the workman which is 15.03.2010 contains date of birth of the workman as 27.05.1959. Similarly, the Form-B of the 
workman does not contain the date of its preparation. Attestation Form prepared on 07.11.2009 contained the date of 
birth of the workman as 27.05.1959. Thus, it is established that there are two sets of documents with the management 
containing two sets of dates of birth of the workman. In such a situation, it was incumbent on the management to 
enquire into this controversy and settle it. The case of the management and submission of the Learned Counsel on this 
point is that the workman himself signed his date of birth in the records maintained by management, which contained 
his date of birth as 05.07.1954. We will have to look into first declaration with respect to date of birth of the workman 
which was made by him at the time of his first appointment in 1978. It may be taken as most accurate, those date of 
birth declared is 27.05.1959. 


It comes out that the date of birth of the workman 05.07.1954 crept for the first time in the list prepared by 
the President and thereafter it was entered into some of the records of the management after the workman was granted 
permanent status. 


It has been submitted from the side of management that the workman accepted his changed date of birth and 
now started agitating against this at fag end of his career just before his superannuation which is not permitted in law. 
Learned Counsel has referred to Single Bench of Hon’ble High Court of M.P. in the case of Surendra Singh vs. State 
of M.P., 2007 (1) MPLJ 286, in this case the workman filed application for correction of his date of birth after 32 
years of service, which he was not permitted. In another case State of U.P. vs. Shivnarayan Upadhyaya, (2005) 6 
SCC 49, referred to by Learned Counsel for management, when the entry regarding date of his birth was challenged 
by the workman on the eve of retirement, Hon’ble Supreme Court observed that Courts and Tribunals should be slow 
in issuing direction for correction of date of birth unless there is clinching and unimpeachable evidence in this regard. 
Also held that in such cases, challenge to date of birth should normally not be entertained when they are made at the 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7089 


eve of retirement. In another reported decision of Hon’ble Supreme Court, in the case of Union of India vs. Harnam 
Singh, (1993) 2 SCC 162, it has been held that when a limitation for seeking change in date of birth is provided, 
claims barred by limitation, should not be entertained except for valid reasons. 


The referred cases can be distinguished on facts. In the case in hand, the workman has been consistently 
agitating for correction of his date of birth. 


Learned Counsel for workman has relied on judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Sarjoo 
Prasad v/s General Manager & Anr., Case No. 377/1981, SCC 544. In this case the Hon’ble Supreme Court has 
referred to and relied on this judgment in the case of State of Orissa v/s Dr. (Miss) Binapani Dei & Ors., AIR 1967 
SC 1269 and has held that date of birth of employee, once accepted by employer cannot be altered without giving him 
an opportunity of hearing and has further held the superannuation of the employee on the basis of his altered date of 
birth against law. The same view has been taken by Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Hari Singh v/s State of 
Bihar, 2000 SC (L & S) 832, proposition of law laid down by Hon’ble Apex Court in these referred cases will apply 
in the case in hand. 


On the basis of above discussion, action of the management of Bhilai Steel Plant, in altering the date of birth 
of the workman Gowdi Satyam from 27.05.1959 to 05.07.1954 and superannuating him on the basis of his altered 
date of birth, is held without authority and in violation of law. Consequently, the workman is held entitled to be 
reinstated from the date he was superannuated by the management and to be deemed in service till the date of 
superannuation on the basis of his date of birth 27.05.1959 with all back wages and pre as well post retiral benefits, 
payable to his legal representatives, by management within 30 days from the date of publication of award, failing 
which interest @ 6% per annum from the date of award till payment. 


On the basis of above discussion and findings, the reference deserves to be answered as follows:- 
AWARD 


Holding the action of management of Bhilai Steel Plant, Iron Ore Complex, Dalli Rajhara, Distt- Balod in 
not correcting the date of birth of Sh. (८ Satyam, Staff Attendant, from 05.07.1954 to 27.05.1959 is against law and 
arbitrary. He is entitled to be reinstated from the date from which he was superannuated by the management and to 
be deemed in service till the date of superannuation on the basis of his date of birth 27.05.1959 with all back wages 
and pre as well post retiral benefits, payable to his legal representatives, by management, within 30 days from the 
date of publication of award, failing which interest @ 6% p.a. from the date of award till payment. 


Connected case No. A-01/2014 also stands disposed accordingly.

outsourced employees and further they are getting the sign on the receipt of Rs. 13,500/-. Claimant has raised his

case that he has been deployed as Supervisor at the MMTC office through the Prominent House Keeping agency 1.6.

done under the influence of the Respondent no. 2 & 3. When the workman went for joining at Manesar, it is utter 
shock to workman when he was not allowed to enter the premises and not allow to join the services. He further
