submitted that he is still under the employment of the respondent management. They fail to make the payment of June 
2018 to till date. He made prayer that award be passed of the amount of Rs. 2,72,000/- and direct the management to 
join his duty at MMTC at Lodhi Colony. 


2. Management no. 1, 2, 3 & 4 have already been proceeded exparte vide order dated 27.04.2022. 
Management-5 has filed its written statement stating that application filed by the claimant is prima facie, 
misconceived, devoid of any justification and jurisdiction. He further submitted that claim is not maintainable as the 
claimant was working with the respondent in a capacity of Supervisor and he was deployed at one of the clients of the 
respondent. The duties of the claimant was to manage and regulate day-to-day affairs of the answering respondent 
with his team, preparing duty rosters allocating duties and shifts for subordinates and takes decision independently to 
satisfy the client of the respondent who were engaged by the answering respondent and performing their duty under 
supervision and control of the claimant. He was authorized to assign the duty to the employees who were working 
under him, he was also authorized to sanction leave to his subordinate. The duties performed by the claimant being 
educative, creative administrative, managerial, supervisory, imaginative in nature thus the claimant do not fall within 
the prescribed categories laid down in section 2(s) of the Act. He also submitted that claim filed by the claimant is not 
maintainable as the claimant did not work for the respondent for a period of 240 days in a calendar year. He submitted 
that claim filed by the claimant is liable to be dismissed. 


3. Claimant has filed the rejoinder denying the averment made by the management in his written statement and 
affirmed the facts made in his claim statement. 

4. After completion of the pleadings vide order dated 13.04.2023, following issues have been framed: 

(1) Whether the proceeding is maintainable. 

(1) Whether the claimant is a workman as defined under section 2(s) of the 1.10 Act. 


(1) Whether the claimant had worked for 240 days in a calendar year preceeding to his alleged termination. 


(IV) Whether the service of the claimant was illegally terminated by the managements. 
(V) To what other relief the parties entitled to, and from whom and from which date? 
5. In order to prove its claim, claimant had tendered his affidavit in evidence affirming the facts made in his 


claim statement stating that he was working as a Supervisor. He was cross-examined where he admitted that he was 
appointed by prominent housekeeping i.e. M-5 on 02.07.2018 and performed his duty till 31.03.2019. He admitted 
that he was working in the capacity of supervisor and there were 23 to 25 Safai Karamchari staffs including one 
female workman were working under his supervision. 


6. Examination in chief and cross-examination of the witness has also been recorded. 


7. I have heard the argument at par. After going through the testimony of this witness, this tribunal has noticed 
that the claimant has nowhere mentioned that he was a workman either in his claim statement or in the affidavit of 
evidence. The claimant who was present himself admitted that he was a Supervisor and his job was to supervise the 
workmen. 


8. To invoke the jurisdiction of this tribunal, first the claimant has to assert that he was a workman within the 
definition of Section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Section 2(s) is required to be reproduced herein: 


2 [(s) “workman” means any person (including an apprentice) employed in any industry to do any manual, 
unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward, whether the terms 
of employment be express or implied, and for the purposes of any proceeding under this Act in relation to an 
industrial dispute, includes any such person who has been dismissed, discharged or retrenched in connection 
with, or as a consequence of, that dispute, or whose dismissal, discharge or retrenchment has led to that 
dispute, but does not include any such person— 


(i) who is subject to the Air Force Act, 1950 (45 of 1950), or the Army Act, 1950 (46 of 1950), or the Navy 
Act, 1957 (62 of 1957); or 


(ii) who is employed in the police service or as an officer or other employee of a prison; or 


(iii) who is employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity; or (iv) who, being employed in a 
supervisory capacity, draws wages exceeding 3 [ten thousand rupees] per mensem or exercises, either by the 
nature of the duties attached to the office or by reason of the powers vested in him, functions mainly of a 
managerial nature.] 


9. Definition of the workman as provided U/s 2(s) is wide enough to include any person as workman in respect 
of his earning, however, section has itself carved out the exception as Clause-(i), (ii), (iii) and (iv). The as exception 
stated that, the person who is employed in the police service or as an officer or other employee of a prison is excluded 
from the category of the workman. The 4" exception stated that, person being employed in a supervisory capacity, 
drawing wages exceeding Rs. 10,000/- per month is excluded from the category of the workman.

10. Claimant has filed the claim under section 2-A of the LD. Act stating that he was transferred to 
Manesar, Gurgaon and not allowing him to join the duty at Manesar amounts to termination. In the entire claim, 
claimant claims to be a supervisor and 23 to 25 Safari Karamchari staffs including one female were working under his 
supervision. 

11. From the averment made in the claim as well as in his affidavit, it appears that the claimant is not a 
workman as defined in the Section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Nowhere has he mentioned either in his 
affidavit or in his claim petition that he had been given designation of Supervisor only by namesake and he was 
working as a workman. He admitted that his job profile was to inspect the work of cleaning staff. 


12. In view of the above discussion, Issue no. 1 & 2 are decided against the claimant and in favour of 
management. 
13. In view of the findings in issue no. 1 & 2, there is no need to decide issue no. 3 & 4. Claim of the claimant 


stands dismissed. Award is accordingly passed. A copy of this award be sent to the appropriate government for 
notification U/S 17 of the I.D Act. File is consigned to record room.

dated 25.11.2022 referred the following Industrial Dispute to this Tribunal for adjudication. 


The schedule mentioned in that order is: 


“Whether the demand of Shri M.P. Musammil, Ex-LIC Development Officer for re-instatement or re- 
appointment with back wage into the service of LIC is justified ? If not, to what relief he is entitled to? 


2: ID called out. Heard of maintainability. Having gone through the record and after hearing the petitioner in 
person and representative of the Respondent / Management, the question that arises to consider at this stage is 
whether the petitioner / claimant comes under the category of workman. 


3. Q.1. The claimant filed a case law in LIC of India & Ors Vs. L. Shan Prasad in WA No.1159 of 2025 dated 
30.11.2025 and stated that, as per the decision of this case, he must be considered as a workman. On perusal of the 
judgment (supra) it reveals that the Hon’ble High Court of Kerala has nowhere discuss the defination of workman and 
that Development Officer comes under the category of the workman or not. The clear case law on the subject is 
Chauharya Tripathi & Ors Vs LIC of India & Ors wherein the Hon’ble Supreme Court held that the Development 
Officers working in LIC are not workmen under Section 2(s) of the Industrial Dispute Act. 


4. In view of the judgment rendered by the Hon’ble Supreme Court, the claimant is not a workman, and 
therefore, this Tribunal has no jurisdiction to decide the lis. 

5. ID is dismissed in for want of jurisdiction and the reference is answered accordingly. 

6. The Petitioner / Claimant may file a petition before the competent authority, if so advised.

As per letter dated 09/01/2012 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification 
No. L-12011/69/2011-(IR(B-D) dt. 09/01/2012. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the demand of the Union for Payment of Bonus to Shri Mohd. Firdaus Sheikh for the period 
from 01/11/1988 to 31/03/2009, is legal and justified? To what relief the workman is entitled to?” 


Notices were issued to both the parties. They appeared and filed their respective statement of claim and 
defense. 


Case of the Workman is that, he was first engaged as a Peon on daily wager by the Bank on 01.11.1988 and 
worked till June, 1996, when disengaged without any notice or compensation. He raised a dispute against his 
disengagement before the Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central), Bhopal. A settlement was made between him 
and the Bank on 13.02.1997 in which the Bank agreed to engage again him as a Daily wager. The Workman was 


7104 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


engaged by Bank as a daily wager. The reference was also made with respect to the dispute raised by him against his 
this disengagement which was registered as R/69/1998. The Workman raised a dispute on 15.09.2019 with respect to 
payment of bonus to him for the period he worked as a daily wager with the Bank. The Management disengaged him 
from 06.12.2009. According to the Workman though he worked from 01.11.1988 to 06.12.2009 he was not paid any 
bonus by the Bank. This action of Bank is unjust, illegal and arbitrary and is in violation of Section 8 and 11 of the 
Payment of Bonus Act. The Workman has prayed that he be held entitled to payment of Bonus for the period claimed 
by him. 


Case of Management is mainly that his claim for payment of bonus from 01.11.1988 to 31.03.2009 is 
barred by Payment of Bonus Act. Management has also denied that Workman has worked with the Management as 
claimed by him and has stated that the Workman had made same claim before the Considering Authority under 
minimum wages Act which was rejected by him, vide order dated 13.05.2013 on the ground that he failed to prove 
that he worked in the Bank from June, 2009 to December, 2009. The Bank has thus prayed that reference be answered 
against the Workman. 


In evidence, the Workman has filed his affidavit as his examination in chief. He has been cross-examined by 
Management. He has filed photocopy documents which are Ex. W-1 Copy of Notification and Messenger, Ex. W-2 
Copy of Application of Workman before Assistant Labour Commissioner, Ex. W-3 and W-5 are different 
representations made by the Workman. Ex. W-6 and W-7 are different payment vouchers paid to the Workman as 
alleged by him, Ex. W-8 is the reference with respect to regularization of the Workman, Ex. W-9 to W-28 are 
different communications made by Bank sending the Workman as Messenger at different places. Ex. W-24 to W-27 
are again payment vouchers, Ex. W-28 is RTI reply. 


Management has examined its witness Manoj Verma by way of filing his affidavit as his examination in 
chief. He has been cross-examined by Workman side. 


There is on record Photocopy of Judgment & Award dated 06.07.2015 in case R/69/1998 relating to 
regularization of the Workman and relating to termination of the services of the Workman w.e.f. 15.12.2009 relating 
to case R/82/2011. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel Mr. Arun Patel for the Workman and Mr. Subh Chaudhaha for 
Management. I have gone through the record as well. 


Reference itself is the issue for determination. 


Section 13, 14, 8, 10 and 22 of the Act are being reproduced as follows : - 
Section 8: Eligibility for bonus.— 


“Every employee shall be entitled to be paid by his employer in an accounting year, bonus, in accordance 
with the provisions of this Act, provided he has worked in the establishment for not less than thirty working days in 
that year.” 


Section 10. Payment of minimum bonus.— 


“Subject to the other provisions of this Act, every employer shall be bound to pay to every employee in 
respect of the accounting year commencing on any day in the year 1979 and in respect of every subsequent 
accounting year, a minimum bonus which shall be 8.33 per cent. of the salary of wage earned by the employee during 
the accounting year or one hundred rupees, whichever is higher, whether or not the employer has any allocable 
surplus in the accounting year: Provided that where an employee has not completed fifteen years of age at the 
beginning of the accounting year, the provisions of this section shall have effect in relation to such employees as if for 
the words “one hundred rupees”, the words “sixty rupees” were substituted.” 


Section 13. Proportionate reduction in bonus in certain cases.— 


“Where an employee has not worked for all the working days in an accounting year, the minimum bonus of 
one hundred rupees or, as the case may be, of sixty rupees, if such bonus is higher than 8.33 per cent. of his salary or 
wage for the days he has worked in that accounting year, shall be proportionately reduced.” 


Section 14. Computation of number of working days.— 


“For the purposes of section 13, an employee shall be deemed to have worked in an establishment in any 
accounting year also on the days on which— 


(a) he has been laid off under an agreement or as permitted by standing orders under the Industrial 
Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 (20 of 1946), or under the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947 (14 of 1947), or under any other law applicable to the establishment; 


(b) he has been on leave with salary or wage; 


(c) he has been absent due to temporary disablement caused by accident arising out of and in the 
course of his employment; and 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7105 


(d) the employee has been on maternity leave with salary or wage, during the accounting year.” 


Section 22. Reference of disputes under the Act.— 


“Where any dispute arises between an employer and his employees with respect to the bonus payable 
under this Act or with respect to the application of this Act to an establishment in public sector, then, such dispute 
shall be deemed to be an industrial dispute within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (14 of 1947), or 
of any corresponding law relating to investigation and settlement of industrial disputes in force in a State and the 
provisions of that Act or, as the case may be, such law, shall, save as otherwise expressly provided, apply 
accordingly”. 


From perusal of these provisions, it is established that firstly, the Workman will be an ‘employee’ and 
Bank is an ‘employer’ within the Act even if the Workman succeeded in proving that he was a daily wager and 
worked with the Bank and secondly, that there is a dispute on the point whether the Workman is entitled to bonus as 
claimed by him which is the subject of the reference in the present case, hence the limitation under Section 21 of the 
Act will not apply in this case. The limitation will apply only when the Management is held under obligation to pay 
certain amount of bonuses to the Workman. 


The judgments and Awards passed by this Tribunal in the aforementioned cases R/69/1998 and 1२/82/2011 
and his disengagement by Bank vide order dated 15.12.2009 was also held unjust and he was directed to be reinstated 
in service with 50% back wages. There is nothing on record to show that these Judgments and Awards have been set- 
aside or modified by any Court or Tribunal. Hence, the findings of the Tribunal with regard to working period of the 
Workman with the Bank in these two cases will operate as res judicata. 


In the light of findings recorded in these two reference cases particularly in Case R/69/1988 in Para 11 of 
the judgment where it is proved that a Workman worked from 1988 to 1996 and again from 1997 to 2009, the action 
of Bank in not awarding him bonus for the period is held unjust and illegal on the part of the Management and the 
Workman is held to be entitled to bonuses from the Management Bank for this period. 


In the light of aforesaid discussion and findings, the reference is answered as follows. 
AWARD 


Holding the demand of the Union for Payment of Bonus to Shri Mohd. Firdaus Sheikh for the period 
from 01/11/1988 to 31/03/2009, is legal and justified on the part of the Management and the Workman is held to be 
entitled to bonus from the Management Bank for this period. 


No order as to cost.

18. All the circulars issued by Department of Posts suggest that since the Petitioner was not in service on 
01.09.1993, he/she is not entitled for absorption. In the case of Dharam Singh Vs. State of U.P & Another in Civil 
Appeal No.8558 of 2018 dated 19.08.2025, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as_under:- 


“17. Before concluding, we think it necessary to recall that the State (here referring to both the Union and the State 
governments) is not a mere market participant but a constitutional employer. It cannot balance budgets on the backs 
of those who perform the most basic and recurring public functions. Where work recurs day after day and year after 
year, the establishment must reflect that reality in its sanctioned strength and engagement practices. The long-term 
extraction of regular labour under temporary labels corrodes confidence in public administration and offends the 
promise of equal protection. Financial stringency certainly has a place in public policy, but it is not a talisman that 
overrides fairness, reason and the duty to organise work on lawful lines. 


18. Moreover, it must necessarily be noted that "ad-hocism" thrives where administration is opaque. The State 
Departments must keep and produce accurate establishment registers, muster rolls and outsourcing arrangements, and 
they must explain, with evidence. why they prefer precarious engagement over sanctioned posts where the work is 
perennial. If "constraint" is invoked, the record should show what alternatives were considered, why similarly placed 
workers were treated differently, and how the chosen course aligns with Articles 14, 16 and 21 of the Constitution of 
India. Sensitivity to the human consequences of prolonged insecurity is not sentimentality. It is a constitutional 
discipline that should inform every decision affecting those who keep public offices running.” 


19. In the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India in SLP No.5580 of 2024 (2024) SCC online 3826 and Shripal & 
Another Vs. Nagar Nigam, Ghaziabad (2025) SCC online 221, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that long-term 
“ad hocism”, is denial of basic parity. The Hon'ble Supreme Court denied the contention of the Respondent that 
daily wagers and temporary employees cannot claim permanent absorption in the absence of statutory Rules. The 
Hon’ble Court further stated that the alleged asserted ban on fresh recruitment, though real, cannot justify indefinite 
daily-wage status or continued unfair practices. 


20. In the present case, the Petitioner has continuously rendered services over several years . The Hon'ble 
Supreme Court has held in the case of Shripal & Another (supra) that Indian Labour Law is 


strongly disfavors perpetual daily-wage or contractual engagements in circumstances, where the work is permanent in 
nature. 


21. Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India (supra) has observed as under:- 


"22. The pervasive misuse of temporary employment contracts, as exemplified in this case, reflects a broader systemic 
issue that adversely affects workers' rights and job security. In the private sector, the rise of the gig economy has led 
to an increase in precarious employment arrangements, often characterized by lack of benefits, job security, workers 
and and fair treatment. Such practices have been criticized for exploiting undermining labour standards. Government 
institutions, entrusted with upholding the principles of fairness and justice, bear an even greater responsibility to avoid 
such exploitative employment practices. When public sector entities engage in misuse of temporary contracts, it not 
only mirrors the detrimental trends observed in the gig economy but also sets a concerning precedent that can erode 
public trust in governmental operations. 


7110 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


25. It is a disconcerting reality that temporary employees, particularly in government institutions, often face 
multifaceted forms of exploitation. While the foundational purpose of temporary contracts may have been to address 
short-term or seasonal needs, they have increasingly become a mechanism to evade long-term obligations owed 
employees. These practices manifest in several ways: 


Misuse of "Temporary" Labels: Employees engaged for work that is essential, recurring, and integral to the 
functioning of an institution are often labelled as "temporary" or "contractual," even when their roles mirror those of 
regular employees. Such misclassification deprives workers of the dignity, security. and benefits that regular 
employees are entitled to, despite performing identical tasks. 


Arbitrary Temporary Termination: employees are frequently dismissed without cause or notice, as seen in the present 
case. This practice undermines the principles of natural justice and subjects workers to a state of constant insecurity, 
regardless of the quality or duration of their service. 


Lack of Career Progression: Temporary employees often find themselves excluded from opportunities for skill 
development, promotions, or incremental pay raises. They remain stagnant in their roles, creating a systemic disparity 
between them and their regular counterparts, despite their contributions being equally significant. 


Using Outsourcing as Institutions Shield: to increasingly resort outsourcing roles performed by temporary employees, 
effectively replacing one set of exploited workers with another. This practice not only perpetuates exploitation but 
also demonstrates a deliberate effort to bypass the obligation to offer regular employment. 


Denial of Basic Rights and Benefits: Temporary employees are often denied fundamental benefits such as pension, 
provident fund, health insurance, and paid leave, even when their tenure spans decades. This lack of social security 
subjects them and their families to undue hardship, especially in cases of illness, retirement, or unforeseen 
circumstances." 


22. The learned counsel for the Respondent argued that no appointment order was issued to the Petitioner, and 
thus no permanent status is allowable to the Petitioner. But the non-issuance of appointment order does not erase the 
entitlement of the Petitioner since the Petitioner has worked for several years and not days.

following directions:- 


The Petitioner’s service shall stand regularized with effect from the date of removal/denial from service 
and the Petitioner shall be reinstated into service within a period of three months with 50% back wages and 
consequential & other attendant benefits.

selection-cum-seniority. The third condition suggests that appointment of existing part-time Casual Labourers, 
engaged on or before 01.09.1993, on the basis of selection-cum-seniority. 


It is true that the Respondent department never constituted any committee to select persons who conferred with 
temporary status by preparing list of selection cum seniority. 


17. All the circulars issued by Department of Posts suggest that since the Petitioner was not in service on 
01.09.1993, he/she is not entitled for absorption. In the case of Dharam Singh Vs. State of U.P & Another in Civil 
Appeal No.8558 of 2018 dated 19.08.2025, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as_ under:- 


“17. Before concluding, we think it necessary to recall that the State (here referring to both the Union and the State 
governments) is not a mere market participant but a constitutional employer. It cannot balance budgets on the backs 
of those who perform the most basic and recurring public functions. Where work recurs day after day and year after 
year, the establishment must reflect that reality in its sanctioned strength and engagement practices. The long-term 
extraction of regular labour under temporary labels corrodes confidence in public administration and offends the 
promise of equal protection. Financial stringency certainly has a place in public policy, but it is not a talisman that 
overrides fairness, reason and the duty to organise work on lawful lines. 


18. Moreover, it must necessarily be noted that "ad-hocism" thrives where administration is opaque. The State 
Departments must keep and produce accurate establishment registers, muster rolls and outsourcing arrangements, and 
they must explain, with evidence. why they prefer precarious engagement over sanctioned posts where the work is 
perennial. If "constraint" is invoked, the record should show what alternatives were considered, why similarly placed 
workers were treated differently, and how the chosen course aligns with Articles 14, 16 and 21 of the Constitution of 
India. Sensitivity to the human consequences of prolonged insecurity is not sentimentality. It is a constitutional 
discipline that should inform every decision affecting those who keep public offices running.” 


18. In the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India in SLP No.5580 of 2024 (2024) SCC online 3826 and Shripal & 
Another Vs. Nagar Nigam, Ghaziabad (2025) SCC online 221, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that long-term 
“ad hocism’”, is denial of basic parity. The Hon'ble Supreme Court denied the contention of the Respondent that 
daily wagers and temporary employees cannot claim permanent absorption in the absence of statutory Rules. The 
Hon’ble Court further stated that the alleged asserted ban on fresh recruitment, though real, cannot justify indefinite 
daily-wage status or continued unfair practices. 


19. In the present case, the Petitioner has continuously rendered services over several years . The Hon'ble 
Supreme Court has held in the case of Shripal & Another (supra) that Indian Labour Law is 


strongly disfavors perpetual daily-wage or contractual engagements in circumstances, where the work is permanent in 
nature. 


20. Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India (supra) has observed as under:- 


"22. The pervasive misuse of temporary employment contracts, as exemplified in this case, reflects a broader systemic 
issue that adversely affects workers' rights and job security. In the private sector, the rise of the gig economy has led 
to an increase in precarious employment arrangements, often characterized by lack of benefits, job security, workers 
and and fair treatment. Such practices have been criticized for exploiting undermining labour standards. Government 
institutions, entrusted with upholding the principles of fairness and justice, bear an even greater responsibility to avoid 
such exploitative employment practices. When public sector entities engage in misuse of temporary contracts, it not 
only mirrors the detrimental trends observed in the gig economy but also sets a concerning precedent that can erode 
public trust in governmental operations. 


25. It is a disconcerting reality that temporary employees, particularly in government institutions, often face 
multifaceted forms of exploitation. While the foundational purpose of temporary contracts may have been to address 
short-term or seasonal needs, they have increasingly become a mechanism to evade long-term obligations owed 
employees. These practices manifest in several ways: 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7115 


Misuse of "Temporary" Labels: Employees engaged for work that is essential, recurring, and integral to the 
functioning of an institution are often labelled as "temporary" or "contractual," even when their roles mirror those of 
regular employees. Such misclassification deprives workers of the dignity, security. and benefits that regular 
employees are entitled to, despite performing identical tasks. 


Arbitrary Temporary Termination: employees are frequently dismissed without cause or notice, as seen in the present 
case. This practice undermines the principles of natural justice and subjects workers to a state of constant insecurity, 
regardless of the quality or duration of their service. 


Lack of Career Progression: Temporary employees often find themselves excluded from opportunities for skill 
development, promotions, or incremental pay raises. They remain stagnant in their roles, creating a systemic disparity 
between them and their regular counterparts, despite their contributions being equally significant. 


Using Outsourcing as Institutions Shield: to increasingly resort outsourcing roles performed by temporary employees, 
effectively replacing one set of exploited workers with another. This practice not only perpetuates exploitation but 
also demonstrates a deliberate effort to bypass the obligation to offer regular employment. 


Denial of Basic Rights and Benefits: Temporary employees are often denied fundamental benefits such as pension, 
provident fund, health insurance, and paid leave, even when their tenure spans decades. This lack of social security 
subjects them and their families to undue hardship, especially in cases of illness, retirement, or unforeseen 
circumstances." 


21. The learned counsel for the Respondent argued that no appointment order was issued to the Petitioner, and 
thus no permanent status is allowable to the Petitioner. But the non-issuance of appointment order does not erase the 
entitlement of the Petitioner since the Petitioner has worked for several years and not days. 


AWARD 


In view of the foregoing discussion, the appeal filed by the Petitioner is liable to be allowed with the 
following directions:- 


The Petitioner’s service shall stand regularized with effect from the date of removal/denial from service 
and the Petitioner shall be reinstated into service within a period of three months with 50% back wages and 
consequential & other attendant benefits. 


The reference is answered accordingly. 
Record be consigned to the record room.

dated 12.01.2023 referred the following Industrial Dispute to this Tribunal for adjudication. 


The schedule mentioned in that order is: 


“1, Whether the demands of Tamilnadu Toll Gate Employees Federation vide letter dated 12.08.2022 and Sengurichi

what directors, if any, are necessary in this respect ?

Federation, Ulundurpet that the termination of 56 workers is illegally done by the management of National Highways 
Authority of India, Trichirappalli (Principal Employer) / Trichy Tollway Private Limited / M/s SKM Contractor & 
Service Pvt. Ltd. / M/s Lakshmi Security Services / M/s Racy Projects is proper, legal and justified? If yes, to what 
relief the disputant is entitled and what directors, if any, are necessary in this respect?” 


2. On receipt of the above reference dated 12.01.2023 from the appropriate Government, the dispute was 
registered as ID No. 4/2023 and due notices were issued to both the parties for their appearance fixing the case to 
01.05.2023. Neither the Petitioner (Petition No. 1 and 2) nor any Counsel / Authorized Representative turned up 
resulting further adjournments to 26.06.2023 and 20.07.2023. The Petitioners did not turn up whereas the 27 Party 
(17, 2" and 37 Respondent filed Vakalat Nama. It reveals from the body of reference that while the appropriate Govt. 
sent the reference dated 12.01.2023 to this Tribunal for adjudication, copies of the reference were sent to the 
Petitioners and all the opposite parties. It is therefore well presumed that both parties must have received the 
reference. Even then, in the interest of justice, the Petitioners were once again directed to appear and to file claim 
statement fixing the case to 02.07.2025 and 25.08.2025. The Petitioner (Petitioner No.1 and 2) did not turn up nor was 
any authorized representative of the counsel on his behalf present. The claim statement was not furnished in any 
manner by the Petitioner (Petitioner Nol and 2). The R4 and R5 were not present, whereas R1 to R3 were present. It 
reveals the Petitioners, despite of sufficient opportunity choose not to appear or to file claim statement and 
documents. 


3. In the circumstance it deems proper not to re-list the case for the same purpose to any other date which 
would be wastage of the valuable time of this Tribunal. The case was reserved for Final Order. 


4. In view of the discussion held supra, it is crystal clear that the petitioners have got no interest to proceed with 
the case. Thus, the Tribunal is not in a position to adjudicate the dispute as referred by the Appropriate Government, 
as there exists no Industrial Dispute for adjudication as per the reference. 


5. In the result the reference is answered against the petitioners. 
An Award is passed accordingly.

6. Heard the learned counsel appearing for either side and perused the records. The point that arises for 
consideration is “whether the employee of the Respondent is entitled for reinstatement into service along with all

7. The Petitioner Shri P.Seenivasan has stated in his claim statement that he had entered into service of the 
Respondent in the year 2007. The fact of continuous service is established by the Petitioner by adducing oral 
evidence as WW1 and filing proof of affidavit and the documents which were marked as Ex.W1 to W19. 


8. The Respondent in its reply admitted this fact that Petitioner was engaged with the Department, but stated 
that engagement was on daily wage basis and not against any MTS vacancies. The Petitioner was not a permanent 
employee and there was no employer-employee relationship exists between the Respondent and the Petitioner. The 
Respondent further stated that no appointment or engagement order was issued to the Petitioner and as per circular 
dated 01.11.1995 and 08.11.1995, casual labourers in employment upto 01.09.1993 were only eligible to be 
conferred with temporary status and the Petitioner was not working on 01.09.1993 with the Department and 
therefore, they are not entitled for any absorption. 


9. The learned counsel for the Respondent further submits that Multi Tasking Staff Recruitment Rules, 2010 
dated 12.12.2010 is not applicable to the Petitioner. As per circular dated 01.11.1995 and 08.11.1995 the following 
conditions must be fulfilled:- 


a) Temporary status on or before 01.09.1993; 
b) Full time casual labourer engaged on or before 01.09.1993 & 
c) Part-time casual labourer engaged on or before 01.09.1993. 


10. The learned counsel for the Respondent contended that Petitioner was not engaged through employment 
exchange and no appointment letter was issued. He further stated that assumption of the Petitioner that he/she works 
against the post of MTS is incorrect. The learned counsel further stated that there was no relationship of employer- 
employee between the Respondent and Petitioner, hence the question of notice or protection u/s.25F of the Industrial

watch & ward, gardening, cleaning etc. are now part of duties assigned to MTS, the existing practice of engaging

01.12.2010. The Petitioner was engaged prior to this circular dated 19.11.2010. 


16. The next document filed by the Respondent and marked as Ex.M6 is a circular issued by Ministry of 
Communications & IT, Department of Posts dated 27.01.2011 regarding filling up of vacancies on the basis of latest 
recruitment rules for the post of MTS, wherein it was directed to observe the following conditions: - 


“i) (a) 25% by appointment of Casual Labourers conferred with temporary status on the basis of Selection- 
cum-seniority failing which by, 


(b) Appointment of existing Casual labourers engaged on or before 1.9.1993 working, for full hours viz. 5 
hours, on the basis of selection-cum-seniority failing which by, 


(c) Appointment of existing part-time Casual Labourers, engaged on or before 1.9.1993, on the basis of 
selection-cum-seniority failing which by, 


(d) Direct recruitment as per the scheme circulated by the Department of Posts from time to time. 


, 


ii). 75% by direct recruitment as per the scheme circulated by the Department of Posts from time to time.’ 


17. This circular clearly suggests that 25% of persons must be appointed from casual labourers, who has been 
conferred with temporary status on the basis of selection-cum-seniority. The second condition suggests appointment 
of existing Casual labourers engaged on or before 1.9.1993 working, for full hours viz. 8 hours, on the basis of 
selection-cum-seniority. The third condition suggests that appointment of existing part-time Casual Labourers, 
engaged on or before 01.09.1993, on the basis of selection-cum-seniority. 


It is true that the Respondent department never constituted any committee to select persons who conferred with 
temporary status by preparing list of selection cum seniority. 


18. All the circulars issued by Department of Posts suggest that since the Petitioner was not in service on 
01.09.1993, he/she is not entitled for absorption. In the case of Dharam Singh Vs. State of U.P & Another in Civil 
Appeal No.8558 of 2018 dated 19.08.2025, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as_under:- 


“17. Before concluding, we think it necessary to recall that the State (here referring to both the Union and the State 
governments) is not a mere market participant but a constitutional employer. It cannot balance budgets on the backs 
of those who perform the most basic and recurring public functions. Where work recurs day after day and year after 
year, the establishment must reflect that reality in its sanctioned strength and engagement practices. The long-term 
extraction of regular labour under temporary labels corrodes confidence in public administration and offends the 
promise of equal protection. Financial stringency certainly has a place in public policy, but it is not a talisman that 
overrides fairness, reason and the duty to organise work on lawful lines. 


18. Moreover, it must necessarily be noted that "ad-hocism" thrives where administration is opaque. The State 
Departments must keep and produce accurate establishment registers, muster rolls and outsourcing arrangements, and 
they must explain, with evidence. why they prefer precarious engagement over sanctioned posts where the work is 
perennial. If "constraint" is invoked, the record should show what alternatives were considered, why similarly placed 
workers were treated differently, and how the chosen course aligns with Articles 14, 16 and 21 of the Constitution of 
India. Sensitivity to the human consequences of prolonged insecurity is not sentimentality. It is a constitutional 
discipline that should inform every decision affecting those who keep public offices running.” 


7122 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


19. In the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India in SLP No.5580 of 2024 (2024) SCC online 3826 and Shripal & 
Another Vs. Nagar Nigam, Ghaziabad (2025) SCC online 221, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that long-term 
“ad hocism”, is denial of basic parity. The Hon'ble Supreme Court denied the contention of the Respondent that 
daily wagers and temporary employees cannot claim permanent absorption in the absence of statutory Rules. The 
Hon’ble Court further stated that the alleged asserted ban on fresh recruitment, though real, cannot justify indefinite 
daily-wage status or continued unfair practices. 


20. In the present case, the Petitioner has continuously rendered services over several years . The Hon'ble 
Supreme Court has held in the case of Shripal & Another (supra) that Indian Labour Law is 


strongly disfavors perpetual daily-wage or contractual engagements in circumstances, where the work is permanent in 
nature. 


21. Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India (supra) has observed as under:- 


"22. The pervasive misuse of temporary employment contracts, as exemplified in this case, reflects a broader systemic 
issue that adversely affects workers' rights and job security. In the private sector, the rise of the gig economy has led 
to an increase in precarious employment arrangements, often characterized by lack of benefits, job security, workers 
and and fair treatment. Such practices have been criticized for exploiting undermining labour standards. Government 
institutions, entrusted with upholding the principles of fairness and justice, bear an even greater responsibility to avoid 
such exploitative employment practices. When public sector entities engage in misuse of temporary contracts, it not 
only mirrors the detrimental trends observed in the gig economy but also sets a concerning precedent that can erode 
public trust in governmental operations. 


25. It is a disconcerting reality that temporary employees, particularly in government institutions, often face 
multifaceted forms of exploitation. While the foundational purpose of temporary contracts may have been to address 
short-term or seasonal needs, they have increasingly become a mechanism to evade long-term obligations owed 
employees. These practices manifest in several ways: 


Misuse of "Temporary" Labels: Employees engaged for work that is essential, recurring, and integral to the 
functioning of an institution are often labelled as "temporary" or "contractual," even when their roles mirror those of 
regular employees. Such misclassification deprives workers of the dignity, security. and benefits that regular 
employees are entitled to, despite performing identical tasks. 


Arbitrary Temporary Termination: employees are frequently dismissed without cause or notice, as seen in the present 
case. This practice undermines the principles of natural justice and subjects workers to a state of constant insecurity, 
regardless of the quality or duration of their service. 


Lack of Career Progression: Temporary employees often find themselves excluded from opportunities for skill 
development, promotions, or incremental pay raises. They remain stagnant in their roles, creating a systemic disparity 
between them and their regular counterparts, despite their contributions being equally significant. 


Using Outsourcing as Institutions Shield: to increasingly resort outsourcing roles performed by temporary employees, 
effectively replacing one set of exploited workers with another. This practice not only perpetuates exploitation but 
also demonstrates a deliberate effort to bypass the obligation to offer regular employment. 


Denial of Basic Rights and Benefits: Temporary employees are often denied fundamental benefits such as pension, 
provident fund, health insurance, and paid leave, even when their tenure spans decades. This lack of social security 
subjects them and their families to undue hardship, especially in cases of illness, retirement, or unforeseen 
circumstances." 

22. The learned counsel for the Respondent argued that no appointment order was issued to the Petitioner, and 
thus no permanent status is allowable to the Petitioner. But the non-issuance of appointment order does not erase the 
entitlement of the Petitioner since the Petitioner has worked for several years and not days. 


AWARD 


In view of the foregoing discussion, the appeal filed by the Petitioner is liable to be allowed with the 
following directions:- 


The Petitioner’s service shall stand regularized with effect from the date of removal/denial from service and 
the Petitioner shall be reinstated into service within a period of three months with 50% back wages and 
consequential & other attendant benefits. 


The reference is answered accordingly. 
Record be consigned to the record room.

India. Sensitivity to the human consequences of prolonged insecurity is not sentimentality. It is a constitutional 
discipline that should inform every decision affecting those who keep public offices running.” 


19. In the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India in SLP No.5580 of 2024 (2024) SCC online 3826 and Shripal & 
Another Vs. Nagar Nigam, Ghaziabad (2025) SCC online 221, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that long-term 
“ad hocism”, is denial of basic parity. The Hon'ble Supreme Court denied the contention of the Respondent that 
daily wagers and temporary employees cannot claim permanent absorption in the absence of statutory Rules. The 
Hon’ble Court further stated that the alleged asserted ban on fresh recruitment, though real, cannot justify indefinite 
daily-wage status or continued unfair practices. 


20. In the present case, the Petitioner has continuously rendered services over several years . The Hon'ble 
Supreme Court has held in the case of Shripal & Another (supra) that Indian Labour Law is 


strongly disfavors perpetual daily-wage or contractual engagements in circumstances, where the work is permanent in 
nature. 


21. Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India (supra) has observed as under:- 


"22. The pervasive misuse of temporary employment contracts, as exemplified in this case, reflects a broader systemic 
issue that adversely affects workers' rights and job security. In the private sector, the rise of the gig economy has led 
to an increase in precarious employment arrangements, often characterized by lack of benefits, job security, workers 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7129 


and and fair treatment. Such practices have been criticized for exploiting undermining labour standards. Government 
institutions, entrusted with upholding the principles of fairness and justice, bear an even greater responsibility to avoid 
such exploitative employment practices. When public sector entities engage in misuse of temporary contracts, it not 
only mirrors the detrimental trends observed in the gig economy but also sets a concerning precedent that can erode 
public trust in governmental operations. 


25. It is a disconcerting reality that temporary employees, particularly in government institutions, often face 
multifaceted forms of exploitation. While the foundational purpose of temporary contracts may have been to address 
short-term or seasonal needs, they have increasingly become a mechanism to evade long-term obligations owed 
employees. These practices manifest in several ways: 


Misuse of "Temporary" Labels: Employees engaged for work that is essential, recurring, and integral to the 
functioning of an institution are often labelled as "temporary" or "contractual," even when their roles mirror those of 
regular employees. Such misclassification deprives workers of the dignity, security. and benefits that regular 
employees are entitled to, despite performing identical tasks. 


Arbitrary Temporary Termination: employees are frequently dismissed without cause or notice, as seen in the present 
case. This practice undermines the principles of natural justice and subjects workers to a state of constant insecurity, 
regardless of the quality or duration of their service. 


Lack of Career Progression: Temporary employees often find themselves excluded from opportunities for skill 
development, promotions, or incremental pay raises. They remain stagnant in their roles, creating a systemic disparity 
between them and their regular counterparts, despite their contributions being equally significant. 


Using Outsourcing as Institutions Shield: to increasingly resort outsourcing roles performed by temporary employees, 
effectively replacing one set of exploited workers with another. This practice not only perpetuates exploitation but 
also demonstrates a deliberate effort to bypass the obligation to offer regular employment. 


Denial of Basic Rights and Benefits: Temporary employees are often denied fundamental benefits such as pension, 
provident fund, health insurance, and paid leave, even when their tenure spans decades. This lack of social security 
subjects them and their families to undue hardship, especially in cases of illness, retirement, or unforeseen 
circumstances." 

22. The learned counsel for the Respondent argued that no appointment order was issued to the Petitioner, and 
thus no permanent status is allowable to the Petitioner. But the non-issuance of appointment order does not erase the 
entitlement of the Petitioner since the Petitioner has worked for several years and not days. 


AWARD 


In view of the foregoing discussion, the appeal filed by the Petitioner is liable to be allowed with the 
following directions:- 


The Petitioner’s service shall stand regularized with effect from the date of removal/denial from service and 
the Petitioner shall be reinstated into service within a period of three months with 50% back wages and 
consequential & other attendant benefits. Ordered accordingly.

reinstatement into service of the Respondent No.1, by setting aside the termination order dated 17.07.2017, with

collection of toll is responsibility of Respondent No.1. The Petitioner has participated in the union activities and the

principles of natural justice and was denied employment since 17.07.2017. It is gross miscarriage of justice and 
there was no application of principles of natural justice.

attend the conciliation proceedings which is still pending. Therefore, it is prayed that impugned order is liable to 
be set aside and the Petitioner is to be reinstated into service with all attendant benefits.

5. The learned counsel for the Petitioner submits that although the Petitioner was issued with suspension 
letter alleging misconducts against the Petitioner, the same was not proved by the Respondent by filing any 
document or memo or charge sheet. Therefore, the very basis of alleged misconduct against the Petitioner does not 
exist in the present case. It appears that the Respondent has reacted against the Petitioner on the false vague 
allegations. The Respondent never appeared before this Tribunal to controvert the statements given by the 
Petitioner in his oral evidence and the affidavit. The letter dated 08.07.2017 sent by the 2" Respondent clearly 
shows that after suspension, no enquiry officer was appointed and no opportunity was provided to the Petitioner. 
Therefore, the order of termination issued by the Respondent is in violative of the principles of natural justice. 


5. The next question for determination that arises is whether the Petitioner is an employee of the National 
Highways Authority of India, who is the principal employer. 


6. In the statement of claim, the Petitioner himself stated that he was appointed by the Respondent No.1 and 
not by Respondent No.3. The Respondent No.3 has provided a contract to Respondent No.1 and 2. The employee 
was appointed under the supervision of Respondent No.2. Thus, the Petitioner is not an employee of Respondent 
No.3 i.e., National Highways Authority of India. 


Ts The next point for determination that arises is what relief the Petitioner is entitled to? 


8. The Petitioner stated in his claim statement that after amendment, Respondent No.4 i.e., Sri Sai Enterprises 
India Private Limited has taken over the charge of Toll Plaza. The Respondent No.4 is an independent contractor 
and it was not employer of the Petitioner. Therefore, it cannot be said that Respondent No.4 has the liability to 
employ the persons who were appointed by the prior contractor. Therefore, the Respondent No.4 is not liable to 
provide service or job to the Petitioner. The Respondent No.1 and 2 are no more contractors of National Highways 
Authority of India. Therefore, it is not possible to pass an order of reinstatement to the Petitioner in the job. But, 
since the Petitioner was not provided neither any opportunity nor issued one month notice or one month salary in 
lieu of notice as provided under section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, is entitled for compensation 
amount of Rs.5.00 lakhs.

passed amounting to Rs.5,00,000/- (Rupees Five Lakhs only) by the Respondent No.1 & 2 to the Petitioner, in lieu 
of order of reinstatement into service. Ordered accordingly. The appeal is allowed on the above terms.

The Petitioner filed this petition u/s.2A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 directly seeking relief of 
reinstatement into service of the Respondent No.2 by setting aside the order of discharge dated 23.08.2016 with 
consequential benefits. 


2. Brief facts of the case are that the Petitioner was engaged by the Respondent No.2 on 19.03.2015 to manage 
Toll plaza to collect toll, carrying out maintenance of the road , maintaining electrical lighting and connections, 
planting and maintaining plants, cleaning roads and providing ambulance service etc. The Respondent denied 
employment to the Petitioner from 24.08.2016 without assigning any reasons. The Petitioner expressed his protest 
through letter dated 28.08.2016. Thereafter, the respondent sent charge sheet dated 30.08.2016 alleging that a van 
bearing no.TN 37 BW 3817 had collided against tanker lorry bearing registration No. TN 01 AX 6675 on the early 
hours of 09.08.2016 and in the course of rescue the Petitioner along with two other employees had removed self- 
motor from the van and committed theft of the same. The Petitioner submitted a letter dated 16.09.2016 requesting 
extension of time, but the Respondent immediately thereafter issued order of suspension cum show cause notice 
dated 09.09.2016. It was further stated that Shri Kandan (Helper) and R.Ayyappan (Driver) had admitted the guilt of 
stealing self-motor from the van and the Petitioner did not inform the Respondent/Management about the theft. The 
Petitioner was provided with two days time for submission of show cause notice in which punishment was proposed. 
It is submitted that the Petitioner had sent a letter dated 14.09.2016 requesting the respondent to furnish copy of the 
video and audio recording in respect of preliminary enquiry proceedings, to tender his explanation. He had made it 
clear that only on furnishing them, he will be able to defend himself. The petitioner also made it clear that he had not 
committed theft of the self -starter motor and that he came to know about the theft only when the management had 
been making enquiry on 23.08.2016. The petitioner made it clear that the allegations levelled against him are foisted. 
The Respondent denied the copy of video and audio enquiry proceedings of Mr.Kandan (Helper) and R.lyyappan 
(Driver) vide letter dated 14.09.2016. The Petitioner submitted the explanation on 16.09.2016 and denied

allegations. But the Respondent/Management in a pre-determined mind vide order dated 30.09.2016 discharged the 
Petitioner from service w.e.f 24.08.2016. 


3. It is further stated that charge of theft against the Petitioner is false. The so called confession of 
Shri Kandan (Helper) and Shri R.Ayyappan (Driver) were not produced. The said two employees do not belong to 
the Respondent and they are contract employees. The Respondent /Management has relied upon the material, which 
was not given to the Petitioner and imposed the capital punishment of discharge. This punishment has been imposed 
by withholding material documents and without conducting proper enquiry and therefore, impugned order is liable 
to be set aside and the Petitioner is to be reinstated into service with all attendant benefits.

2; On perusal of these documents, it is clear that sufficient opportunity was not provided to the Petitioner 
during the enquiry and the charge of theft is not established. The copy of footage of audio/ video enquiry 
proceedings in the case of Shri M.Kandan, Helper & R.Ayyappan, Driver was not provided to the Petitioner. The 
only witness against the Petitioner was the two employees Shri M.Kandan, Helper & R.Ayyappan, Driver. In case, 
the management wanted to confess the offence of theft and to punish the Petitioner on the basis of statements of 
Shri M.Kandan, Helper & R.Iyyappan, Driver, it was essential to provide copy of footage of audio/ video in enquiry 
proceedings. 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7135 


6. Since the establishment of offence of theft was based on no evidence and without providing material 
documents to the employee during the enquiry i.e., copy of footage of audio/ video enquiry proceedings in the case of 
Shri M.Kandan, Helper & R.Ayyappan, Driver, which is in violation of principles of natural justice. Although, the 
Disciplinary Authority has considered the proportionality of punishment, he has considered grave misconduct of 
very serious nature such as theft. But, as I discussed above, charge of theft was not established by conducting fair 
and domestic enquiry before the Enquiry Officer. Since it was essential to adhere to the principles of natural justice 
while conducting fair enquiry, the copy of audio/video recordings of enquiry proceedings in respect of Shri 
M.Kandan, Helper & R.Ayyappan, Driver must have been provided to the Petitioner, but it was not provided so. 
Further, the Petitioner was not given any occasion to cross examine the witnesses, who rendered confessional 
statement before the management. Therefore, the punishment of discharge from service is disproportionate because 
the misconduct was not established. 


7. The Respondent never appeared before this Tribunal to establish the charge of theft and fairness of enquiry 
conducted against the Petitioner. If a domestic enquiry is found to be unfair, the enquiry conducted by the 
Respondent/Management is vitiated and ultimately punishment imposed becomes invalid, consequently, the 
employee is entitled to reinstatement into service . Since the employer failed to justify its action against the 
employee, then punishment inflicted is liable to be set aside and workman is entitled to reinstate into service. 


8. Now, I have to consider back wages to be payable to the employee. The enquiry conducted by the 
Respondent is in violative of principles of natural justice and the employer failed to conduct fair and proper enquiry 
against the employee and even failed to provide extension of time to submit his explanation as requested by the 
employee. Further, the Respondent/Management considered the act of Petitioner as criminal in nature and if it is an 
act of theft, no FIR was registered against the employee and since, it is not essential to seek criminal prosecution of 
the employee, the Respondent/Management chose to initiate departmental action. But, while taking departmental 
action, no fair and proper enquiry was conducted against the Petitioner. In the case of Shankar Dass Vs Union of India 
(1985) SC 772, wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that penalty of dismissal from service imposed upon 
delinquent clerk is whimsical and the power was not exercised fairly, justly and reasonably. Applying the above 
ratio to the present case, since the departmental enquiry conducted by the Respondent/Management against the 
employee is unfair, the order of punishment imposed upon the Petitioner i.e., order of discharge dated 30.09.2016 
becomes invalid in the eye of law. 


AWARD 


The appeal filed by the Petitioner is allowed. The Petitioner is entitled for reinstatement into service of the 
Respondent No.2 with full back wages. The Respondent No.2 is directed to implement the Award within a period of 
one month from the date of receipt of this order.

5 The Petitioner has submitted proof of affidavit in support of her claim and adduced oral evidence as ४०७1 


and documents filed by her were marked as Ex.W1 to W21. The Respondent has also filed its proof of affidavit 
and Shri R.Swaminathan, Assistant Chief Accounts Officer was examined as MW1 and documents on behalf of

6. Heard the learned counsel appearing for either side and perused the records. The point that arises for 
consideration is “whether the employee of the Respondent is entitled for reinstatement into service along with all 
benefits against the management of Department of Postal Accounts & Finance? If not to what relief the 
concerned workman is entitled?” 


7. The Petitioner Mrs.B.Mymoon has stated in her claim statement that she had entered into service of the 
Respondent in the year 2008. The fact of continuous service is established by the Petitioner by adducing oral 
evidence as WW1 and filing proof of affidavit and the documents which were marked as Ex.W1 to W21. 


8. The Respondent in its reply admitted this fact that Petitioner was engaged with the Department, but stated 
that engagement was on daily wage basis and not against any MTS vacancies. The Petitioner was not a permanent 
employee and there was no employer-employee relationship exists between the Respondent and the Petitioner. The 
Respondent further stated that no appointment or engagement order was issued to the Petitioner and as per circular 
dated 01.11.1995 and 08.11.1995, casual labourers in employment upto 01.09.1993 were only eligible to be 
conferred with temporary status and the Petitioner was not working on 01.09.1993 with the Department and 
therefore, they are not entitled for any absorption. 


9. The learned counsel for the Respondent further submits that Multi Tasking Staff Recruitment Rules, 2010 
dated 12.12.2010 is not applicable to the Petitioner. As per circular dated 01.11.1995 and 08.11.1995 the following 
conditions must be fulfilled:- 


a) Temporary status on or before 01.09.1993; 
b) Full time casual labourer engaged on or before 01.09.1993 & 
c) Part-time casual labourer engaged on or before 01.09.1993. 


10. The learned counsel for the Respondent contended that Petitioner was not engaged through employment 
exchange and no appointment letter was issued. He further stated that assumption of the Petitioner that he/she works 
against the post of MTS is incorrect. The learned counsel further stated that there was no relationship of employer- 
employee between the Respondent and Petitioner, hence the question of notice or protection u/s.25F of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 does not arise. 


11. On behalf of the Respondent a circular dated 17.05.1989 has been filed which is marked as Ex.M1, and it 
clarifies the position of casual labourers and part-time casual labourers in para 2, which reads as under: - 


“2. It is hereby clarified that all daily wagers working in Post Offices or in RMS Offices or in Administrative 
Offices or PSD's/MMS under different designations (mazdoor casual labourer, contingent paid staff, daily 
wager, daily rated mazdoor, outsider) are to be treated as casual labourers. Those casual labourers who are 
engaged for a period of 8 hours a day should be described as full-time casual labourers. Those casual 
labourers who are engaged for a period of less than 8 hours a day should be described as part-time casual 
labourers. All other designations should be discontinued.”

12. The Petitioner in the claim statement stated that the work was performed for a period of more than eight hours per 
day. The Respondent witness MW1 in his oral evidence nowhere stated that Petitioner did not perform the work 
about eight or more than 8 hours per day. 


13. The Respondent submitted another circular dated 11.09.1991 which is marked as Ex.M2. The subject of this 
circular is Casual Labourers (Grant of Temporary Status and Regularization) Scheme. This circular did not suggest 
date of appointment of the labourers which means this circular does not impose a condition that the casual labour 
must be in service on a particular date. 


14. The another circular issued by Respondent, Department of Posts, dated 27.11.1995 marked as Ex.M3, 
which suggests that full time casual labourers recruited after 29.11.1989 upto 10.09.1993 may also be considered 
for grant of benefits under the scheme. This circular later specified the particular date i.e., 10.09.1993. 


15. The next document marked as Ex.M5 dated 19.11.2010, which states that no casual labour shall be engaged 
in the administrative office with effect from 01.12.2010. This circular further stated that since the duties of 
waterman, watch & ward, gardening, cleaning etc. are now part of duties assigned to MTS, the existing practice of 
engaging casual labourers as waterman, gardener, watch and ward or any other category shall be dispensed with 
from 01.12.2010. The Petitioner was engaged prior to this circular dated 19.11.2010. 


16. The next document filed by the Respondent and marked as Ex.M6 is a circular issued by Ministry of 
Communications & IT, Department of Posts dated 27.01.2011 regarding filling up of vacancies on the basis of latest 
recruitment rules for the post of MTS, wherein it was directed to observe the following conditions:- 


“1) (a) 25% by appointment of Casual Labourers conferred with temporary status on the basis of Selection- 
cum-seniority failing which by, 


(2) Appointment of existing Casual labourers engaged on or before 1.9.1993 working, for full hours viz. 6 
hours, on the basis of selection-cum-seniority failing which by, 


(c) Appointment of existing part-time Casual Labourers, engaged on or before 1.9.1993, on the basis of 
selection-cum-seniority failing which by, 


(d) Direct recruitment as per the scheme circulated by the Department of Posts from time to time. 


, 


ii). 75% by direct recruitment as per the scheme circulated by the Department of Posts from time to time.’ 


17. This circular clearly suggests that 25% of persons must be appointed from casual labourers, who has been 
conferred with temporary status on the basis of selection-cum-seniority. The second condition suggests appointment 
of existing Casual labourers engaged on or before 1.9.1993 working, for full hours viz. 8 hours, on the basis of 
selection-cum-seniority. The third condition suggests that appointment of existing part-time Casual Labourers, 
engaged on or before 01.09.1993, on the basis of selection-cum-seniority. 


It is true that the Respondent department never constituted any committee to select persons who conferred with 
temporary status by preparing list of selection cum seniority. 


18. All the circulars issued by Department of Posts suggest that since the Petitioner was not in service on 
01.09.1993, he/she is not entitled for absorption. In the case of Dharam Singh Vs. State of U.P & Another in Civil 
Appeal No.8558 of 2018 dated 19.08.2025, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as_under:- 


“17. Before concluding, we think it necessary to recall that the State (here referring to both the Union and the State 
governments) is not a mere market participant but a constitutional employer. It cannot balance budgets on the backs 
of those who perform the most basic and recurring public functions. Where work recurs day after day and year after 
year, the establishment must reflect that reality in its sanctioned strength and engagement practices. The long-term 
extraction of regular labour under temporary labels corrodes confidence in public administration and offends the 
promise of equal protection. Financial stringency certainly has a place in public policy, but it is not a talisman that 
overrides fairness, reason and the duty to organise work on lawful lines. 


18. Moreover, it must necessarily be noted that "ad-hocism" thrives where administration is opaque. The State 
Departments must keep and produce accurate establishment registers, muster rolls and outsourcing arrangements, 
and they must explain, with evidence. why they prefer precarious engagement over sanctioned posts where the work 
is perennial. If "constraint" is invoked, the record should show what alternatives were considered, why similarly 
placed workers were treated differently, and how the chosen course aligns with Articles 14, 16 and 21 of the 
Constitution of India. Sensitivity to the human consequences of prolonged insecurity is not sentimentality. It is a 
constitutional discipline that should inform every decision affecting those who keep public offices running.” 


19. In the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India in SLP No.5580 of 2024 (2024) SCC online 3826 and Shripal & 
Another Vs. Nagar Nigam, Ghaziabad (2025) SCC online 221, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that long-term 
“ad hocism”, is denial of basic parity. The Hon'ble Supreme Court denied the contention of the Respondent that 
daily wagers and temporary employees cannot claim permanent absorption in the absence of statutory Rules. The 


7142 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


Hon’ble Court further stated that the alleged asserted ban on fresh recruitment, though real, cannot justify indefinite 
daily-wage status or continued unfair practices. 


20. In the present case, the Petitioner has continuously rendered services over several years . The Hon'ble 
Supreme Court has held in the case of Shripal & Another (supra) that Indian Labour Law is 


strongly disfavors perpetual daily-wage or contractual engagements in circumstances, where the work is permanent in 
nature. 


21. Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India (supra) has observed as under:- 


"22. The pervasive misuse of temporary employment contracts, as exemplified in this case, reflects a broader systemic 
issue that adversely affects workers’ rights and job security. In the private sector, the rise of the gig economy has led 
to an increase in precarious employment arrangements, often characterized by lack of benefits, job security, workers 
and and fair treatment. Such practices have been criticized for exploiting undermining labour standards. Government 
institutions, entrusted with upholding the principles of fairness and justice, bear an even greater responsibility to 
avoid such exploitative employment practices. When public sector entities engage in misuse of temporary contracts, 
it not only mirrors the detrimental trends observed in the gig economy but also sets a concerning precedent that can 
erode public trust in governmental operations. 


25. It is a disconcerting reality that temporary employees, particularly in government institutions, often face 
multifaceted forms of exploitation. While the foundational purpose of temporary contracts may have been to address 
short-term or seasonal needs, they have increasingly become a mechanism to evade long-term obligations owed 
employees. These practices manifest in several ways: 


Misuse of "Temporary" Labels: Employees engaged for work that is essential, recurring, and integral to the 
functioning of an institution are often labelled as "temporary" or "contractual," even when their roles mirror those of 
regular employees. Such misclassification deprives workers of the dignity, security. and benefits that regular 
employees are entitled to, despite performing identical tasks. 


Arbitrary Temporary Termination: employees are frequently dismissed without cause or notice, as seen in the 
present case. This practice undermines the principles of natural justice and subjects workers to a state of constant 
insecurity, regardless of the quality or duration of their service. 


Lack of Career Progression: Temporary employees often find themselves excluded from opportunities for skill 
development, promotions, or incremental pay raises. They remain stagnant in their roles, creating a systemic 
disparity between them and their regular counterparts, despite their contributions being equally significant. 


Using Outsourcing as Institutions Shield: to increasingly resort outsourcing roles performed by temporary 
employees, effectively replacing one set of exploited workers with another. This practice not only perpetuates 
exploitation but also demonstrates a deliberate effort to bypass the obligation to offer regular employment. 


Denial of Basic Rights and Benefits: Temporary employees are often denied fundamental benefits such as pension, 
provident fund, health insurance, and paid leave, even when their tenure spans decades. This lack of social security 
subjects them and their families to undue hardship, especially in cases of illness, retirement, or unforeseen 
circumstances." 

22. The learned counsel for the Respondent argued that no appointment order was issued to the Petitioner, and 
thus no permanent status is allowable to the Petitioner. But the non-issuance of appointment order does not erase 
the entitlement of the Petitioner since the Petitioner has worked for several years and not days. 


AWARD 


In view of the foregoing discussion, the appeal filed by the Petitioner is liable to be allowed with the following 
directions: - 


The Petitioner’s service shall stand regularized with effect from the date of removal/denial from service and the

3. As per the claim statement, the case of the Petitioner is that he entered as casual labourer in the
